articles.title: US national debt keeps rising after years of tax cuts – and this will make policymaking all the more difficult
articles.author: Hinckley Jones-Sanpei, Public Policy Researcher, University of Denver
paras: Democrats, set to take over Congress with robust majorities, will face at least one expensive obstacle to their policy agenda: a national debt that now equals the size of the U.S. economy.

Clocking in at US$32 trillion, this debt-to-GDP ratio of 100% would likely raise alarms for other countries. But it attracted relatively little attention in an election season dominated by concerns over the economy and the cost of living.

Debt has grown to these levels because over the past 25 years, the federal government has been spending more than it collects in taxes. Even as the U.S. economy grew, lawmakers have cut taxes repeatedly, sometimes with bipartisan support, instead of paying down debt.

The series of tax cuts since 2001 has added over $10 trillion to the debt, according to an analysis of Congressional Budget Office data by the Center for American Progress. In fact, without these series of cuts, the debt-to-GDP ratio would be decreasing, the study found.

The debate over taxation often falls along partisan lines, with arguments focusing on which income groups are affected or the potential impact on economic growth. But as a public policy scholar, I believe that important context is often overlooked. Under conditions of strong gross domestic product growth and low debt, tax cuts may have a relatively benign fiscal impact. But today, because debt as a share of GDP is so much higher, and interest rates are steeper, the cost of adding new debt is much greater than 15 or 20 years ago, whether through additional spending or through tax cuts.
I believe Democrats will have to wrestle with this math as they try to advance a policy agenda focused on affordability that minimizes the risk of further borrowing.
Proponents of fiscal austerity argue that lower spending should accompany tax cuts so that debt doesn’t rise.
U.S. federal spending, however, has remained relatively flat – outside of emergencies like the 2009 recovery package and COVID-19 stimulus funds – even as GDP has risen.

At the same time, each round of tax cuts over the past quarter century has actually gotten smaller over time if they’re assessed as a share of GDP, as a study by the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan think tank, noted.

President Ronald Reagan’s 1981 tax cuts were the most expensive in history, reducing annual federal revenue on average by 2.9% of GDP, according to the Tax Foundation’s analysis. The next two biggest cuts occurred in 1945 and 1948, when the government rolled back the wartime hikes that helped pay for World War II. President Barack Obama’s 2012 legislation, extending most of the temporary tax cuts passed under President George W. Bush, comes in fourth at 1.8% of GDP, while cuts passed under President Lyndon Johnson in 1964 rank fifth.
Coming in sixth place at 1.2% of GDP: President Donald Trump’s sweeping policy and tax legislation in 2025, which made permanent most of his 2017 tax cuts.

While the Trump cuts amounted to a relatively small share of GDP, they had a much larger effect on the national debt due in part to the higher cost of borrowing. The original 2017 legislation was projected to increase public debt from 91.2% to 97.1% of GDP by 2027, with an overall 10-year cost of $1.5 trillion. That was based on the assumption the cuts would expire after 2025.

But just like the earlier round of Bush tax cuts, Congress was loathe to let those provisions lapse. In 2025, the narrow Republican majority pushed through Trump’s legislation that extended or made permanent the 2017 cuts.

The Congressional Budget Office, the independent government scorekeeper of legislation, estimated that the 2025 bill would add another $3.4 trillion over 10 years. And it projected that increasing deficits would push debt to 116% of GDP by the end of 2034.
Why deficits and economic growth matter so much
A basic calculation explains when debt stays stable, and when it does not.

If a government runs a “primary” budget surplus – that is, excluding interest payments – and economic growth is higher than the interest rate on government bonds, debt remains stable. The problem for the U.S. is that budget deficits have been growing faster than the economy, while interest payments on government debt are rising as well.

This math explains why the trajectory of economic growth is so important in understanding the impact of tax cuts. When taxes were cut after World War II, the economy was booming, the U.S. carried little debt, and reducing taxes didn’t further add to it. By contrast, government spending ballooned under Reagan, thanks in large part to defense outlays. Combined with lower tax revenue due to tax cuts, the national debt tripled during Reagan’s time in office.

In 2000, the economy was surging again. That was the last time the U.S. took in more tax revenue than it spent and began paying down the debt. President George W. Bush cited this surplus to justify his first round of major tax cuts in 2001, which also drew support from some Democrats.

It remains to be seen how much leverage the results of the midterms will grant Democratic lawmakers in the next two years as they try to enact legislation under Trump. But I believe lawmakers of all stripes will have to confront the hard choices that the U.S. national debt imposes on policy directions going ahead, thanks to a long series of decisions made over the past quarter century.

articles.title: When a Walmart closes, what happens to nearby stores?
articles.author: Vivek Astvansh, Associate Professor of Quantitative Marketing and Computational Data Science, Binghamton University, State University of New York
paras: Shoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay, while competitors find cause to celebrate.
Among critics of the big-box behemoth, a long-held assumption is that once a Walmart disappears, shoppers seeking groceries, household goods, meals and services will flow to businesses down the road.
But what if the economic downside of a closure is bigger?

We are marketing scholars who have studied dozens of Walmart closures in the United States. We found that nearby stores saw a slump in both monthly shopper traffic and sales revenue by roughly a quarter in contrast to comparable stores near Walmart locations that remained open. Our sample covered 39 Walmart stores that closed across 20 states from 2019 to 2026.

This finding suggests a large retailer can play two roles at once. Walmart competes with neighboring businesses for shopper visits and spending. But it can also act as an anchor, giving people a reason to travel to a shopping area in the first place. When that anchor disappears, the loss of shared shopper traffic can outweigh the benefit of having one less competitor.

Our finding underscores that retailers don’t operate as isolated dots on a map. Shoppers often decide where to go before deciding which stores they’ll visit once they get there. A trip to Walmart can generate a stop at a nearby restaurant, pharmacy, salon, specialty retailer or service business.

Economists call this kind of benefit an agglomeration effect: Businesses can gain from being near other businesses because the location itself attracts shoppers. Shopping center owners have long recognized this logic by using prominent stores to anchor a mix of tenants.

Other researchers have found that Walmart’s entry into a shopping area causes sales in nearby existing stores to drop. But these shops can adjust their product assortment, prices and promotions to mitigate this effect, follow-up studies suggest. What has not been studied until now is what happens when a Walmart store – or any other anchor store – closes.

A Walmart closure creates a tug-of-war between two forces, we argue. Competitive relief helps nearby businesses because a formidable rival is gone. But agglomeration loss hurts them because fewer shoppers have a reason to visit the area.
This means a store can capture a larger share of local consumer demand after Walmart leaves and still end up worse off if the total pool of shoppers arriving in the area shrinks enough.
What happened after a Walmart closed

We combined closure dates with monthly store-level shopper traffic and spending data. For each closed Walmart, we identified nearby non-Walmart businesses and compared their post-closure performance with that of businesses near Walmarts that stayed open.

We discovered not just a sizable decline in both shopper traffic and sales revenue after closure but a worsening trend in both over time. Specifically, following a Walmart’s closure, nearby stores experienced a roughly 5% drop in the following month and 6% in the month thereafter. The decline keeps getting worse, reaching about 17% in the ninth month and 20% a year after the anchor store closes.

That parallel movement in traffic and sales matters. If nearby stores were simply selling less to the same number of shoppers, we would expect spending per visit to fall. Instead, what was also happening is that fewer shoppers visited nearby businesses after the anchor disappeared.
In short, competitive relief didn’t overcome the loss of traffic that would have been generated by trips to the anchor store. But not all nearby businesses were affected equally.

Stores that competed more directly with Walmart had better post-closure sales than noncompeting stores. That is what we would expect if competitive relief is real: Grocery stores and other close substitutes are better positioned to capture some of the displaced consumer demand.

Well-known brand stores also fared relatively better than unbranded businesses. A recognizable brand can give shoppers an independent reason to visit, reducing reliance on traffic generated by the nearby anchor. And stores surrounded by more outlets with its own brands also had more favorable post-closure sales.

Another important factor is digital reach. Not surprisingly, the more a business engages with customers online, the less it depends on people physically traveling to a cluster of stores. We found that stores with a higher share of revenue from online orders saw a less severe drop in sales after a Walmart closed.
These patterns suggest that managers have options and can act: Opening another location or expanding online sales can protect a retailer from an anchor closure.
Why a store closing can become a neighborhood shock

A large retailer decides whether to keep a store open based primarily on what makes sense for its own portfolio. But the surrounding businesses face a different calculation. A location that looks weak from the anchor retailer’s perspective can still drive valuable traffic to neighboring stores.

That creates what economists call an externality – a positive or negative effect of an economic activity that impacts other parties even though market prices don’t reflect it. In this case, some of the economic value produced by an anchor sits outside the anchor’s own sales and profits.

For neighboring businesses, the lesson is not to assume that a powerful competitor’s departure will create a windfall. Rather, managers need to know how many customers arrive because of the broader shopping destination, not merely how much their store’s products overlap with the anchor’s.

Meanwhile, commercial property owners should treat losing an anchor as more than risking an empty storefront. It can also hurt the rest of their portfolio by reducing consumer demand. Replacing the tenant quickly matters, but so does finding a replacement that can generate trips to the area.

Finally, local governments and economic development organizations need to understand that a major retail closure may affect businesses with no contractual relationship to the closed store. So their responses should extend beyond the vacant property itself – whether it’s speeding redevelopment, coordinating with local businesses and property owners to improve shoppers’ access, or helping create a new destination that restores shopper traffic.

articles.title: You’ve been told to prep three days of food, but moving past day four will need stronger supply chains
articles.author: Ebru Surucu-Balci, Assistant Professor in Circular Supply Chains, University of Bradford
paras: The UK government’s recent “Be Ready” campaign advises households to keep a three-day supply of food and drink in case of emergency. Sales of bottled water and tinned foods have soared, as households ready themselves for a powerful storm, a long power cut or a cyber-attack.
And preparing for three days of self-resilience seems like a sensible measure. But what happens on day four?
The hope would be that order is restored, with no further need for people to rely on their own supplies.
But what if the supply chains we rely on every day have not recovered in time? After all, it’s not as if they’re not vulnerable to attack.
Part of this vulnerability is down to companies using what we call a “just-in-time” strategy, where goods are produced or delivered just at the point that they are needed.

This means companies holding minimal stock levels, which reduces costs and waste. It can also involve using the same software across the supply chain to improve visibility and ensure accurate forecasting of demand.
And while all of these measures dramatically improve efficiency, one failure can hit several supply chains at once.

For example, in 2024, a cyber-attack on a supply-chain software company disrupted warehouse management systems and the supply of fresh produce for UK supermarkets. In 2025, a refrigerated logistics firm was targeted, causing widespread delays and cancellations of deliveries.
Also in 2025, a cyber-attack on M&S led to a five-day suspension of online sales and empty shelves in stores.

Then in October 2026, hackers targeted French supermarkets, causing refrigeration units to overheat and spoil millions of euros worth of food. The UK’s food supply chain was affected by a similar attack on supermarkets across Europe at the start of November.
This system, which seems to be so easily disrupted, was built for good and sensible reasons.

When businesses over order, or make inaccurate predictions about demand, food spoils. And research shows that poor coordination around production, logistics and sales leads to significant food wastage.

Sleek digital supply chains are designed to fix this problem. Forecasting software (which predicts who needs what and when) and automated ordering mean less food sits in a warehouse going off. That is a real gain, environmentally and economically.

The challenge is that these efficiency improvements can limit the capacity to absorb unforeseen disruption. When stores hold only a few days’ stock and every step depends on software, there is little to fall back on when something – a hacker, a flood or a war – cuts off supplies.

The UK government has been warned about this, with the National Audit Office saying that food supply chains have prioritised efficiency, keeping costs down for businesses and shoppers, but leaving them vulnerable to shocks.
So, does improving resilience mean giving up efficiency and returning to massive warehouse stockpiles?
After the Russia-Ukraine war disrupted wheat and sunflower oil supplies in 2022, we were part of a team which surveyed over 300 food manufacturers that relied on supplies coming from the region.

The firms that coped best did two things. They worked hard to eliminate waste in their processes (by reusing and recycling materials, for example), and they quickly reorganised, finding alternative suppliers.
For supermarkets then, the lesson is to plan for disruption as seriously as they plan for efficiency. Two changes can be implemented in a short period.

The first is localisation, where sourcing more food from the UK will help shorten supply chains and reduce dependency on distant suppliers and long transport routes. The second is diversification, using more than one supplier for key products and more than one software or logistics provider.
In this way, a single failure cannot stop food from reaching the shelves. A chain with more than one route to the shelf is much harder to break.
Household supply chains matter too. Building up long-life supplies gradually, and using and replacing them in rotation, stops preparation from becoming waste.
Stocking up at home is a sensible first line of defence, and those who can follow the government’s advice should. But three days of tins cannot keep a country fed.

What happens on day four depends on decisions made long before any emergency: how much buffer stock the food system keeps, how many routes it has to the shelf, and how quickly firms can adapt. Resilience has to be built into the food system, not just people’s cupboards.

articles.title: Paraguay’s bank collapse brought down a president – and exposed as myth the nation’s status as a ‘Dubai of South America’
articles.author: Joel E. Correia, Associate Professor in Human Dimensions of Natural Resources, Colorado State University
paras: It started on Nov. 3, 2026, when millions of Paraguayans trying to access the Ueno banking app found they could no longer get their money. In a matter of days, the financial situation escalated into political crisis, in which the country’s president was ousted, placed under house arrest and charged with several corruption-related crimes.

The political and financial crisis exposes a central contradiction in Paraguay’s recent economic development. Ueno, a bank celebrated for expanding financial access to ordinary Paraguayans, grew through unusually close relationships with political elites and public institutions. And while the Ueno crisis came as a shock, there were clear warning signs.

As scholars with expertise in various aspects of Paraguay’s contemporary political, economic and environment development, we believe the collapse raises troubling questions about who benefits from financial modernization, who controls it and who bears the risks when it fails. The political relationships through which financial institutions grow, regulators exercise authority and public resources are entrusted to private companies are crucial national concerns, especially in a country that has presented itself internationally as a model of economic stability.
A bank that grew faster than scrutiny

Founded as a digital lender in 2021, Ueno attracted customers with mobile banking and cash-back offers. Its expansion brought useful services to people underserved by conventional banks, including rural customers. Ueno also expanded the credit card market to low-income customers, an unprecedented move compared to previously restricted banking practices.

As Ueno expanded, Paraguay increasingly attracted investors drawn by its low taxes, economic stability and business-friendly policies. Promoted by some as a “Dubai of South America,” the country also became a magnet for conservative influencers, particularly from Brazil, who contrasted Paraguay’s economic model with the purported mismanagement of left-wing governments elsewhere in the region. Indeed, under President Santiago Peña, Paraguay has been one of Latin America’s most enthusiastic allies of the Trump administration and its expansive regional vision.
But beneath the financial stability, Ueno stood at the precipice of a much deeper problem.

The central bank finally acted after accounting adjustments left Ueno’s solvency ratio below half the legal minimum. But problems had surfaced earlier. That included a supervisory report put out by the bank regulators in June 2026 that described roughly US$146 million in loans to three companies linked to Grupo Vázquez, Ueno’s controlling shareholder. Some companies had been transferred to group employees; supervisors questioned the collateral and ultimate use of the funds.
That these warning signs went unheeded raises a related question of why regulators didn’t have a better handle on the situation and were not better able to contain the exposure.

In any case, Ueno’s problems were exposed in dramatic fashion on Nov. 2, when the central bank placed Ueno into resolution, a process similar to bankruptcy but managed directly by Paraguay’s central bank. The lender, which says it has nearly 3 million customers – about half of the country’s population – halted transactions.

The crisis quickly ensnared the governing party. Peña, an economist by training who was elected president in 2023 and had close ties to the bank, resigned on Nov. 5. The Senate then voted unanimously to remove him from office, thereby stripping Peña of his parliamentary immunity. He was swiftly put under house arrest, charged with corruption and succeeded by his Vice President Pedro Alliana, who was sworn in to serve until 2028.
Meanwhile, the crisis has led to widespread protests, including outside Congress, with citizens accusing Peña and the ruling Colorado Party of “stealing” their savings.
When the regulator knows the regulated
Part of the story of Ueno is a tale of the closeness between political and financial elites in Paraguay.

Carlos Carvallo chaired Ueno’s predecessor bank before Peña appointed him Paraguay’s central bank president in 2023. Carvallo resigned on Nov. 3 and has since been charged with the same corruption crimes as Peña. For its part, the Paraguayan central bank says Carvallo recused himself from any Ueno decisions.

Yet the potential conflicts of interest ran much deeper. Peña previously directed Banco Basa, linked to Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, who retains considerable influence and was instrumental in helping push Peña out of office. Finance Minister Carlos Fernández Valdovinos also served on Basa’s board. Local reporters had documented these revolving-door relationships early in Peña’s term.

Peña reportedly held a 1.58% stake in Ueno Holding, which shared its principal shareholder, Grupo Vázquez, with Ueno bank. His brother Francisco held shares in Luxembourg-based U Holdings, an indirect shareholder in the bank. Another shareholder was Juan Carlos López Moreira, Cartes’ former chief of staff. Both brothers exited in 2025.
Peña has denied any wrongdoing, while prosecutors are examining allegations concerning his former business interests and his administration’s financial supervision.

The inclusion of significant reserves of public funds made these connections especially consequential. Ueno held approximately $850 million in public funds, including $355 million from the country’s social security system, IPS, including health and retirement funds. It amounted to roughly 9% of IPS’s investment portfolio.

Under Peña-appointed chairman Jorge Brítez, IPS relaxed eligibility requirements for bank deposits in 2023 and removed a capital-based exposure limit in 2024. Over the same period, its deposits at Ueno rose sharply. Grupo Vázquez’s technology firm ITTI won at least $2.3 million in state contracts after Peña took office, versus $675,000 before. ITTI attributed the increase to business expansion and denied a conflict of interest.
Together these ties and regulatory changes raise important questions about regulatory capture and other potential conflicts of interest.
What the growth figures leave out

Paraguay’s economic gains are real. In August, the International Monetary Fund projected 4.4% growth in 2026 following 6.6% in 2025. Moody’s granted the country’s debt investment-grade status in 2024, and S&P followed in 2025. Hydroelectric power exports, agriculture and new infrastructure continue to underpin the economy.

Washington is also drawing Paraguay more firmly into its regional economic strategy. On Oct. 23, the country became the 26th signatory to the Pax Silica Declaration, an initiative involving critical minerals, hydropower and advanced computing infrastructure. While the announcement did not specify financing commitments, it shows how Paraguay’s resources and perceived political predictability are being positioned as strategic assets.

But growth figures and credit ratings say little about who shapes financial oversight or bears the costs of banking failures. Paraguay’s legacies of political patronage make it necessary to examine political and corporate connections and changes to public-fund investment rules.
The social toll and the Colorado question

Paraguay has been here before. Between 1995 and 1998, 13 banks and 35 financial firms closed, with direct costs estimated by the IMF at 10% to 13% of the country’s GDP. This preceded a smaller bank crisis in the early 2000s. Both ordeals exposed weak supervision and connected lending.

Paraguay’s deposit guarantee, which covers balances up to about $38,000, is meant to limit depositor losses, and the Paraguayan Central Bank insists that failure is isolated in the latest case. Yet account transfers have already strained the system, producing outages at several banking institutions.

Yet for most Paraguayans, the crisis was experienced not through technical financial or macroeconomic indicators but at the stark level of seeing from their phones that they couldn’t access their money. Wages, pensions and savings froze simultaneously. Young Ueno employees burned their company cards outside the Labor Ministry, demanding unpaid wages.
Riot police used pepper spray and rubber bullets against depositors marching on Congress. For small businesses that banked and paid staff through Ueno, the real economy stopped.

This widespread anger challenges the ruling party’s claims to the economic vision they cite as the engine for future growth. Whether it leads to institutional change or a reshuffle within the Colorado Party remains an open question. The test is how Paraguayan legislators and regulators will move forward and whether they separate banking supervision and public deposits from partisan and business networks.

In any case, the myth of the “Dubai of South America” has come under serious scrutiny. While the protests were noteworthy, the Colorado Party has for now managed to resolve its own internal crisis by quickly sacrificing key political elites, including the president.

Marco Castillo Ph.D., Paraguayan sociologist, recent graduate and former director of research at the Center for Latin American, Latino and Caribbean Studies at Graduate Center CUNY, and Sheyla Rios Galeano, a Ph.D. Student in human dimensions of natural resources, Colorado State University, contributed to this article.

articles.title: Voters rejected data centers in dozens of communities, fueling the narrative that opposition to the AI infrastructure contributed to the 2026 blue wave
articles.author: Barbara A. Trish, Professor of Political Science, Grinnell College
paras: Data centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections.
A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development.

The centers also may have played a role in several high-profile contests. In Ohio’s race for a U.S. Senate seat, Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign. Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state. As governor-elect, she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers.

According to NBC exit poll data, 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%.

Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure, housing the computing resources used to train AI models. These massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use, higher utility bills and environmental degradation, outweigh the benefits.

I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns.

Before the midterms, it had already appeared to be disrupting some partisan alignments. Following those historic elections, which have thoroughly shaken up America’s political geography, the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms.
Disrupting political polarization

In contrast to many other issues, concern about data centers is relatively bipartisan. The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities. Opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines.

Local ballot measures restricting data centers also cut across traditional political alignments. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points.

The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota, population around 800. With a data center project already in progress, political and economic leaders prevailed in arguing that restrictions would cut into local revenue and stifle economic development more generally.

Exit polls taken during the midterm elections also detected a degree of bipartisanship. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote, approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. Exit polls, however, should be interpreted with care, given their methodological limitations.
These responses hint at why the narrative that opposition to data centers helped fuel the Democrats’ historic midterm victory emerged right away.

The seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing a diverse kind of resistance: environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests.

Some of the bipartisanship around this issue has even seeped into Congress. Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote. The bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers.

Similar concerns killed the Senate version, a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change.
Brookings Institution scholars anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements.

As the midterm elections approached, candidates up and down the ballot blanketed the airwaves and digital platforms with ads against data centers. President Donald Trump pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.”
Some Republican candidates walked a fine line between responding to voters’ concerns and not alienating the president.

It matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and so far, the reported evidence is limited. We need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. That voters considered data centers important says nothing about which direction they leaned. And despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than 600 proposed data centers that are slated to be built.

What does matter is that many people apparently are accepting the narrative because that alone will affect politics and the economy. Consider Elon Musk’s post on Nov. 4 on X, his social media platform: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” and the sell-off of data center-related stocks the next day.

As the 2028 presidential primaries come into focus, I believe we should expect to see many Democratic and Republican hopefuls emphasizing their support for data center restrictions and bans as they throw their hats into the ring.

articles.title: Flesh-eating screwworm is spreading in the US, threatening livestock and wildlife – hunters can be the first line of defense
articles.author: Jacob Dykes, Assistant Professor of Wildlife Management, Mississippi State University
paras: For the first time in over 50 years, an infestation of the flesh-eating fly known as the New World screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax) is spreading on the U.S. mainland, and it is putting livestock and other animals at risk.
The New World screwworm doesn’t just attack cattle. All warm-blooded animals are susceptible, including deer and elk, as well as small game, waterfowl and pets.
That means hunters headed to the field this fall may be the most important line of defense for spotting this destructive parasite and keeping it from spreading further.

As co-directors of the Mississippi State University deer lab, we believe the country’s millions of hunters can serve as a powerful early warning system by keeping a close eye on the state of wildlife they see. Wildlife agencies are already asking them to be vigilant and report any signs of screwworm infestations.
The problem with screwworm

Unlike other blowflies, New World screwworm larvae feed on living tissue rather than dead tissue. They lay eggs in open wounds or mucosal openings, such as the eyes and nose of livestock, deer or elk.

Wounds as small as tick bites or scratches, as well as natural openings such as the umbilical stump on newborns or on deer’s pedicles, where their antlers grow and are shed, can attract these parasites.
Once the eggs hatch, the maggots burrow into the animal’s flesh and feed, enlarging the wound and attracting more flies. Over time, this leads to infection and death.
How the US eradicated screwworm in the past
All warm-blooded animals are susceptible to the New World screwworm, but America has seen firsthand the harm they can cause to livestock.
In the 1950s, livestock producers in the U.S. Southwest lost up to US$100 million annually to New World screwworm infections, equivalent to over $1 billion today.

The nation was eventually able to eradicate the New World screwworm from the mainland in 1966 using a combination of treating infected animals and raising hundreds of millions of sterilized male flies and releasing them in infested areas.

The New World screwworm has a life cycle of only about 21 days, and each female mates only once. Because of that, inundating areas with sterile male flies for a few months, which equates to a few generations of flies, can eradicate a screwworm population.

Over time, sterile flies were used to push the New World screwworm further south, where they had been contained behind the Darién Gap, Panama’s narrow border region with Colombia. Sterile flies kept the parasite south of Panama for years, but the movement of cattle and wildlife likely brought it north again. Since 2022, the parasites have been reproducing and moving farther northward. There have been hundreds of detections in Mexico and now in the U.S.
The Florida Key deer infestation

Wildlife have received far less attention than livestock during screwworm infestations, with one exception: In July 2016, the New World screwworm was detected in the Florida Keys in an endangered deer population: the Florida Key deer (Odocoileus virginianus clavium).

At the time, the Florida Key deer population was estimated at only about 800 to 1,000 individuals. Because they were endangered and isolated, primarily on the islands of Big Pine Key and No Name Key, they were monitored more closely than most wildlife.

U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service biologists established quarantine zones. They inspected more than 16,900 animals – dogs, cats, a pig and a raccoon were also found with larvae – and they released 150 million sterile flies across the area. The islands lost 9% to 20% of the total Key Deer population, but the New World screwworm was declared eradicated there on March 23, 2017, less than a year after it was discovered.

In June 2026, screwworm was back in the United States. A rancher discovered the first New World screwworm case in a calf near La Pryor, Texas. A few more cases were confirmed in livestock and domestic animals in Texas and New Mexico.

The number of cases in animals had passed 120 as of Nov. 7, 2026, including in two elk reported by hunters in Texas. The U.S. government has started ramping up production of sterile flies to try to keep the parasites from spreading.
Although there have been only a couple of cases reported in wildlife, that isn’t necessarily reassuring.

Wildlife are far more likely to carry the parasite without being detected. Once the screwworm is detected, treatment would also be much more complicated for wildlife than for livestock, because wildlife cannot be treated individually and thus are more dependent on the use of sterile flies to eradicate screwworm.
For this reason, quickly identifying areas with New World screwworm and targeting those areas by releasing sterile flies would be more important than ever.
Tapping an army of conservationists: Hunters
Fortunately, there is an army of conservationists across the country who spend much of their time afield. These conservationists are also known as hunters.

According to the latest U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service National Survey of Fishing, Hunting, and Wildlife-Associated Recreation, nearly 11.5 million hunters pursue big game and spend part of the fall and winter in the field hunting ungulate species such as deer and elk.

White-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) hunters alone are expected to harvest about 6 million deer during the 2026-27 season and will observe millions more. Hunters also review tens of millions of wildlife pictures collected each year by game cameras used for scouting.

That level of surveillance can’t be matched. New Mexico’s Department of Agriculture has already called on hunters to report any suspicious larvae, particularly in Grant and Otero counties, where screwworm has been found in livestock. Hunters of all kinds, everywhere, can help.
What to watch for as a hunter
If you’re a hunter, be on the lookout for wounded animals, especially those with visible maggots, and for unusual behaviors such as restlessness, lethargy, or biting or licking wounds.

Do not move harvested animals from the field if they show signs of a New World screwworm infection. Doing so could further spread the parasite. Instead, contact the area’s state wildlife agency, the U.S. Department of Agriculture office or a local veterinarian immediately.
As hunting seasons get underway across the country, an army of conservationists will be in the field, and they have an important role to play in detecting and managing screwworm’s spread.

Hunters already contribute to conservation through license fees, excise taxes and keeping wildlife populations at healthy densities. In the face of New World screwworm, their observations may be most valuable for protecting livestock.

articles.title: Interest rates are making UK homes less affordable, even as wage rises increase faster than house prices
articles.author: Alper Kara, Head of Department of Economics, Finance & Accounting, Brunel University of London
paras: The Bank of England’s decision to put interest rates up for the first time in over three years could be bad news for prospective homebuyers. Higher borrowing costs risk putting home ownership even further out of reach for many people.
But the numbers aren’t all bad.
Official figures show that annual earnings between 2021 and 2025 increased by 25%, while house prices in England rose by around 15%.
So if wages are going up faster than house prices, why does buying one remain so difficult?
The answer lies partly in the difference between the price of a property and the actual cost of buying it.

Over the past two decades, UK house prices have risen substantially relative to incomes. In the early 2000s in England, they were equivalent to about four times the average annual salary. By 2021, they were around nine times.
There has been some improvement since then. In 2025, the median home in England cost £300,000, equivalent to 7.6 times average annual full-time earnings of £39,300.
When earnings rise faster than house prices, people can potentially save towards deposits more quickly and end up borrowing less.

But what’s less encouraging is the fact that the usual comparison between house prices and earnings overlooks the monthly cost of mortgage repayments. And rising interest rates have made these repayments considerably more expensive.
Consider a couple in which both partners earn the median full-time salary and want to buy a home in England.
In 2021, their combined annual earnings would have been approximately £62,900. If they bought a £250,000 property with a 10% deposit, they would have needed a £225,000 mortgage.
With an interest rate of 1.95% on that mortgage (widely available five years ago), their monthly repayments over 25 years would have been roughly £948, equivalent to 18.1% of their monthly income.
Five years later, things look quite different.
Adjusting for current figures, their combined earnings would have increased by 25% to £78,600, while the property’s value would have risen by approximately 15% to £287,500.

Despite this improvement in house affordability compared to earnings, their mortgage rate would now probably be around 5.65%. This means monthly payments of about £1,612 – 24.6% of their monthly income.
In other words, although earnings have grown faster than house prices, the proportion of income required to pay the mortgage has increased substantially.
Inflation adds another layer of economic pressure. For although earnings have increased, the rising cost of food, energy and transport leaves much less money available for mortgage repayments.

Higher mortgage rates also reduce borrowing capacity, as banks and other lenders assess applicants’ ability to meet repayments alongside their other financial commitments. As a result, some borrowers may qualify for smaller mortgages than they might expect.
These pressures are particularly significant for first-time buyers, who cannot rely on accumulated housing equity, and must often save for a deposit while paying substantial rents.

For a £300,000 property, a 10% deposit requires £30,000, excluding stamp duty, legal fees, or moving expenses. Even households earning good salaries may struggle to save this amount while meeting everyday living costs.
Research shows that this in turn creates a divide between those receiving family financial support and those relying on their own savings.

Higher borrowing costs widen this gap, delaying home ownership or pushing buyers towards smaller properties or cheaper, more distant locations. It can then delay decisions to start a family and limit opportunities to move elsewhere for work.

Despite these challenges, slower house price growth offers grounds for cautious optimism. A sustained period of modest house price growth, alongside stronger earnings, could gradually reduce the gap between property values and incomes.
But if mortgage rates remain high, improvements in property affordability may not translate into lower monthly repayments.
The government’s recent budget offers some relief through a proposed scheme to help first-time buyers with smaller deposits and lower mortgage costs.

Yet without a significant increase in housing supply, such support could just end up pushing up property prices. Making home ownership genuinely more accessible requires sustained income growth, affordable mortgages and increased housing supply.

articles.title: How often should you be working at the office? Here’s what the research suggests
articles.author: Umar Boodoo, Associate Professor, Warwick Business School, University of Warwick
paras: Office attendance from Monday to Friday used to be a pretty standard requirement for many jobs.
But plenty of employees have now developed a taste for working from home. And in response, some of their employers have started to tighten the rules on hybrid work.
Barclays Bank is one of latest big companies to do so, telling thousands of UK staff they must be in the office at least three days a week instead of two.
So what is the right balance for those who split the locations of their working week?

Plenty of research has now been done on that question. And while it does not give a single magic number, the evidence does suggest that the best range is two or three days in the office – on the same days as your colleagues.

For example, in a study involving a large online travel agency in China, more than 1,500 engineers, marketing and finance staff were allowed to work from home on Wednesdays and Fridays, while a control group stayed in the office full time.

Over the following two years of performance reviews, the performance of the hybrid workers was equal in quality to those who stayed in the office. And the ones who worked from home were much less likely to leave the company – especially women and the workers with long commutes.
A smaller experiment at an international development organisation went a step further, by randomly varying how many days 148 staff spent in the office.

Those who came in around two days a week said they had a better work-life balance, more job satisfaction and less isolation than colleagues who came in more or less often. Their performance was unaffected.
These studies (among others) suggest that a week split roughly half and half between home and office costs employers little, while keeping staff happier and more likely to stay.
But there is also evidence that the office time counts, and that some work really does suffer at a distance.

In experiments across five countries, researchers found that video calls can reduce the flow of creative ideas. And an analysis of 20 million research papers and 4 million patents found that remote teams were less likely to produce breakthroughs. The evidence shows that being in the same room matters most when people are coming up with ideas together.

But that doesn’t mean office workers should be together all day every day. In the Chinese travel agency trial, staff in the office three days a week did just as well as those in for five. The extra two days bought nothing measurable in performance – but more resignations.

Yet there is a risk that return-to-office rules set a minimum number of days with no maximum, so that the minimum number creeps up. A study of over 1,000 UK managers, found that employees working from home were less likely to be considered for promotion and pay rises. When being seen is rewarded “at least three days” can quietly become four or five days for those who want to climb the career ladder.
How many days you spend in the office matters less if your colleagues are not there with you.

A study of 48,000 employees at an IT firm found that during hybrid working, innovation suffered the most in teams where office attendance was poorly coordinated. This can mean that people commute in to work, find that their team members or close colleagues are not there, and then spend the day on video calls they could have joined from home. They experience the downsides of office working and get none of the benefit.
Overall then, the research so far on hybrid working suggests a few simple rules:
The aim should be two or three days in the office, and that range should come with a maximum as well as a minimum.
Those days should be the same for for the whole team. The study of UK managers found that the career disadvantages that came with working from home disappeared in teams where it was the norm.
Use office days for the things that benefit from being in the same room, like brainstorming or mentoring new staff. Keep home days for focused work.

No large study has yet directly compared two days in the office with three. But the overall picture is consistent. Two or three coordinated days seems to be the sweet spot, and employers who ask for more should be able to explain exactly what those extra days are for.

articles.title: Florida just voted for lower property taxes – and that could mean cuts in government services and new housing construction
articles.author: Abigail Hall, Professor of Economics, University of Tampa
paras: Many Florida homeowners cheered on Nov. 3, 2026, when more than 60% of voters approved a constitutional amendment to significantly reduce property taxes.

Under the measure, Amendment 3, a homeowner’s tax break known as a homestead exemption would go from the current US$51,400 to $150,000 in 2027 and increase again to $250,000 in 2028. By shielding more of a home’s assessed value from taxation, this exemption effectively lowers homeowners’ tax bills. New Florida residents who buy a home would also reportedly be eligible for a property tax break, but on a more phased-in basis.

But the measure comes with a hefty price tag. The Florida Legislature’s research arm estimated the measure would reduce annual revenue from property taxes by $11.8 billion. This translates to a 30% reduction in revenue for Florida counties and a 13% cut for smaller municipal governments.

While homeowners will get some relief, the budget crunch due to the lower tax revenue will affect other Floridians in more adverse ways. As economists who have been following the debates over Amendment 3, we argue that local governments will struggle to fund basic services with less money. And we expect more sweeping economic consequences as well – including less affordable residential housing and a broader shift of the tax burden away from relatively wealthier homeowners to those who are less well off.
How Amendment 3 would work

Much of the political momentum for Amendment 3 came from a rise in the cost of living and frustration over rising property taxes. These now average just over $3,000 annually but can run much higher for Floridians with more expensive homes.

In addition to raising the homestead tax exemption, Amendment 3 lowers the cap on annual assessments on rental and commercial properties from a 10% increase to a 5% increase. Since property taxes are based on an asset’s assessed value, this language effectively limits but doesn’t rule out tax hikes for businesses.
So landlords, for example, could still see meaningful annual tax increases as their properties go up in value – costs that would likely be passed on to renters.

Amendment 3 makes clear that school-related property taxes are exempt from these tax cuts. It also lists some theoretical limits on how local governments should use tax dollars, as a way to ensure continued funding for essential services such as public safety, infrastructure or obligations for employee retirement benefits.
But it also states that funds may be used for “expenditures approved” by local and county governments – ambiguous wording that suggests these stipulations can be breached.

Florida property taxes are levied and collected by some 640 local government entities. There’s no state income tax, so any reductions in property tax revenue directly affect local and county governments.

With tax revenue slashed, businesses, landlords and owners of other non-homestead properties like second homes would almost certainly see their taxes go up. This is a typical pattern: When governments cut property taxes for some groups, taxes shift to other groups.

This dynamic is likely to play out with local governments as they try to keep revenue stable: Amendment 3 would force them to hike taxes in other areas to make up for the shortfall. This could include increases in state and local sales taxes, an expansion of the list of goods subject to sales taxes, or a hike in “documentary stamp taxes,” which are required on documents such as deeds, bonds and mortgages.

State and local governments could also impose higher fees for specific services, such as solid waste treatment and stormwater utilities. Another option is to hike permits and inspection fees, fuel taxes or other service charges such as vehicle registration fees.

Finally, local governments could raise tourism-related taxes, such as on food, beverages and hotels. But this recourse wouldn’t help counties with limited tourism, and such revenues fluctuate in any event.

In the end, though, essential services would still almost certainly be affected. Funding for police, fire and emergency medical services is primarily the responsibility of local governments, and, for most counties, they make up the largest line item in their annual expenditures. Reducing property taxes would amount to a direct hit, especially in smaller, less-populated counties.

And if local governments do raise sales tax rates to the extent they can, lower-income Floridians will bear a disproportionate burden as they spend much more of their income on consumption. They’re also far more likely to rent than own a home, so any increased rents would take a bigger toll.
A looming affordable housing crunch?

Less noticed in the debate over Amendment 3 was how it would affect the state’s affordable housing shortage. We argue that the structure of the property tax cut will likely create more incentives for counties and developers to build commercial structures instead of more residential housing.

When developers build residential homes, they require a basic level of public services to support residents and the local infrastructure. In fact, property taxes in much of Florida effectively subsidize residential home development: For every dollar that a homeowner pays in property taxes, it costs county governments around $1.20 to provide those services. This gap will only grow when property tax revenues fall.

From the standpoint of local and county governments, then, it may make more sense to focus on commercial or industrial construction as a way to keep tax revenues stable. But with fewer homes built at the expense of business construction – from manufacturing to data centers – the supply squeeze will only drive up prices and rents for the workers who are needed for those jobs.

Now that Amendment 3 is on the books, Florida’s county and local governments will confront major trade-offs. We believe that state officials will come to realize how much of a change has been made – and how quickly their priorities may have to shift.
This article has been corrected to note that the current homestead exemption is $51,400 and that new Florida residents who buy a home are eligible for a property tax break on a phased-in basis.

articles.title: Midterms are bad for incumbents – and even worse when energy prices are high
articles.author: Michael A. Mische, Associate Professor of the Practice of Management and Organization, Marshall School of Business, University of Southern California
paras: As Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “It’s the economy, stupid.” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead. The cost of energy underlies much of the economy, making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise.
Midterm elections have historically been difficult for incumbent presidents and often shift the balance of power in Washington, D.C.

Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control. Prices for crude oil and petroleum products such as gasoline are set on global markets as the results of economic forces of supply and demand. Even the companies that produce oil don’t have as much influence as people might think, because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is transported by ocean tankers, with 20% of global supplies traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on.
When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food, follow. Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally.

Voters pay attention to those changes, and incumbents are less likely to win reelection. For the 2026 midterm election, gasoline prices were the highest of any previous election. That put Republicans in the precarious position of defending their record.
Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices during midterm elections.
Oil embargo, Nixon and Ford

Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political. In retaliation for U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo on the United States. OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month, and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of $4.31 to $10.31 per barrel in March 1974. Nixon’s federal price controls on petroleum didn’t prevent U.S. gasoline prices from increasing 32%.
When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office. Inflation was 12.3%, and gas prices were still high.
Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “Whip Inflation Now,” or WIN, campaign. But Republicans lost 48 House seats and five Senate seats.
“WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were over 60 cents a gallon – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3.49. Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter.
In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. stayed high and even climbed slightly. Inflation hit 9% in 1978.

In the 1978 midterm election, Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats. Inflation continued to climb, and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were twice what they had been in 1976. Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan.

Reagan implemented “Reaganomics” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and removing the remaining price controls on petroleum. By the mid-1980s, increased oil production from U.S. and non-OPEC nations led to an oil glut, lowering the average price of crude oil and U.S. gasoline price from previous highs.
In the 1982 midterms, Republicans lost 26 seats in the House and gained one in the Senate.

Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms. Though crude oil prices were $15 a barrel and gas had dropped to 82 cents a gallon, Republicans lost five seats in the House and eight in the Senate.

In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had risen about 24% from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018. And gas prices were up 22%. In the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate.

Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U.S. economy. U.S. crude oil production fell as gasoline demand plummeted by 40%. Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups.
And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. rose by 66%, from $2.11 to $3.52 per gallon.
Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies.

Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of $0.17 to $0.42 per gallon.

But other Biden policy moves made it harder to increase energy supplies. He canceled the Keystone XL pipeline project that would have brought more petroleum into the U.S. and suspended new oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the Gulf of Mexico. He also recommitted the U.S. to the Paris climate accord, under which countries have promised to cut their greenhouse gas emissions, generally meaning moving away from fossil fuels as an energy source.
In June 2022, inflation reached 9.1%, a 40-year high. And U.S. gasoline prices reached an all-time high of $4.929 per gallon; adjusted for inflation, that’s $5.60 a gallon today.

The 2022 midterm election wasn’t as bad for Democrats as they might have feared, though it wasn’t a success: The party lost nine House seats and one Senate seat. That’s a reminder that energy prices aren’t the only factor in voters’ minds when they are casting ballots.

During the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, crude oil prices fell 4.5%, U.S. oil production rose 3.3%, from 13.3 million to 13.7 million barrels per day, and the AAA national average price of regular unleaded gasoline fell 4.5%, from $3.12 to $2.98 per gallon.

On Feb. 28, 2026, U.S. military action against Iran disrupted Middle Eastern oil production and oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Initially, shipment volume plummeted, though by the end of September it had recovered to 82% to 92% of prewar levels.

Overall, Middle Eastern crude oil exports are averaging around 24 million barrels a day, exceeding prewar levels in part because of increased use of pipelines out of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Because of the war with Iran, AAA’s national average price of unleaded regular gasoline has increased by almost 40%, from February’s $2.98 price to $4.15 a gallon as of Nov. 3, 2026.
As the preelection polling had suggested, voters held Trump accountable for high gasoline and grocery prices, as well as an unpopular war.

It was a reminder of a basic economic and political principle: When the economy is doing well, voters are more likely to support incumbents and their parties. And when voters are pessimistic about the economy’s future, they are inclined to vote against incumbents and their parties.

articles.title: Why a company donating $20,000 a month counts for more than $240,000 once a year in the eyes of customers
articles.author: Yanyi Leng, Assistant Professor of Marketing, Colorado State University
paras: People tend to think more highly of companies that give to charity on a monthly or weekly basis rather than donating an annual lump sum worth the same amount.

This is what I and five other marketing researchers found when we conducted seven studies involving more than 150,000 people. The Journal of Marketing Research, which is peer-reviewed, published our article on the results in early 2026. My co-author Alexander B. Park and I led the team.
Our goal was to discover whether the way a company communicates with the public about its donations affects how much credit it gets from consumers for those gifts.

Across seven studies, we found that companies earn more goodwill when they give consistently – say, US$20,000 a month – instead of making a single $240,000 gift. On average, consumers also said they were more likely to buy from those companies.

To test this premise, we did two real-world studies. First, we partnered with GiftAMeal, a U.S. company that runs a free app for diners. Each time someone takes a photo of their meal at a participating restaurant and shares it on social media, GiftAMeal donates to a local food bank.

We ran two versions of GiftAMeal’s Facebook ad, which together reached 67,576 people. One said the company “donated 25,000 meals every month” last year. The other said it “donated 300,000 meals” last year. Both were true, and everything else about the ads was the same. We found that people who saw the monthly version were about 21% more likely to click on the ad.

Next, we worked with Salt + Smoke, a Midwestern barbecue restaurant. When we emailed 75,514 customers who subscribed to its newsletters, half read that the company would give $5,000 a month from September through December to a small, local charity that supports early childhood education programs. The other half read that it would make a one-time donation of $20,000.

Subscribers who read about the monthly donation pledge were nearly twice as likely to click through to the restaurant’s website as those who read about the one-time gift pledge even though the total was the same.

Then we ran online experiments with more than 7,400 people to learn why and when consistent giving makes people view a company more favorably. We found that, on average, when a company gives monthly, people see its charitable support as a more genuine commitment to the causes.

U.S. companies gave nearly $44 billion in 2025 alone. And this kind of giving is popular with the public. In a 2022 survey, 88% of Americans said it’s important for companies to make the world a better place.

Companies frequently promote their donations with the largest numbers they can muster. For example, Microsoft announced that the software giant and its employees donated $256 million in 2025; Walmart and its foundation say they have donated $2 billion in 2026.

Yet boasting about big numbers may not impress people as much as emphasizing the consistency of donations. This may help explain why companies often struggle to convey their charitable efforts in ways that win people over.

Even if companies give only once a year, they can indicate that they are engaged in a steady pattern of giving. For example, they can make their annual gifts on Giving Tuesday every year. Donating on the same day or as part of the same fundraising campaign every year can signal an ongoing commitment, not a one-off.
We don’t yet know how long the reputational boost companies may get from recurring donations might last, or whether those donations can translate into long-term customer loyalty.

It’s also possible that what we found would not apply during emergencies. For example, consumers might be happy to see a company make one big gift right after a hurricane when a local community’s needs are immense.

Along with Park and Cynthia Cryder, a Washington University in St. Louis marketing professor, I’m now studying other ways that corporate philanthropy can affect how much credit companies get for doing good. So far, we’ve found that companies may earn less goodwill when they ask customers to chip in to their charitable campaigns. People seem to expect companies to carry more of the load themselves.
The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work.

articles.title: Fireworks provide a few minutes of joy, but the economic and environmental costs last much longer
articles.author: Narmin Nahidi, Assistant Professor in Finance, University of Exeter
paras: Every Bonfire Night, people pay for a box of fireworks so their friends and family can enjoy the colourful display. Within a few minutes, it’s all over. But the price on the box doesn’t reflect the hidden costs. The smoke inhaled by neighbours, the animals disturbed or the public services called out when things go wrong.

It’s not a question about whether fireworks celebrations are enjoyable, but whether the people enjoying them are aware of – or actually paying for – their full cost. Economists call this a “negative externality”. A purchase benefits the buyer and seller, but some of its costs fall on people outside that transaction. Fireworks offer a particularly visible example because the enjoyment is concentrated in time while the consequences are spread among households, public services and wildlife. As a finance researcher, I think this concept is overlooked in the fireworks debate.

Consider injuries. Figures show that 123 hospital admissions in England attributed to fireworks in 2024–25. That is not a count of everyone injured: cases treated without hospital admission are excluded. Preventing such injuries may not cut the NHS budget, but it can free clinical time for other patients. In an overstretched health service, that is an economic benefit even if it never appears as a saving in the Treasury’s accounts.

Pollution creates another unpriced cost. The UK’s official air-quality monitoring has recorded short-lived spikes in fine particles around Bonfire Night, although bonfires also contribute and weather affects how quickly smoke disperses. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs assigns a central estimated damage cost of £114,411 per tonne of fine particulate emissions (known as PM2.5), expressed in 2025 prices to account for inflation. This is not a figure for fireworks: calculating that would require information about their emissions and who is exposed. It does show why a product can have an environmental cost that never appears on its receipt.
Nature belongs on the balance sheet

The damage is not limited to human health. In a peer-reviewed Dutch study, researchers found that approximately 1,000 times as many birds were flying during New Year’s Eve fireworks as on ordinary nights. The disruption extended several miles from the displays. The exact scale cannot be transferred to British Bonfire Nights, but the finding challenges the idea that fireworks affect only those who choose to watch.

Birds forced into sudden flight expend energy and lose opportunities to rest. Pets and livestock may also be distressed. Alongside noise and smoke, spent casings and other waste leave a physical footprint. Sustainability means considering these effects, not simply asking how much carbon a celebration emits.

Yet putting nature on an economic balance sheet requires care. The value of healthy ecosystems is real, but we should not invent a monetary figure for fireworks-related wildlife damage when credible national estimates are lacking. Some effects can be quantified; others must still inform decisions even without an exact price.

Fireworks also create value. They support retailers, display organisers and cultural celebrations, including Bonfire Night, Diwali and New Year. The UK government’s 2026 consultation reports that fireworks imports averaged £27 million a year from 2021 to 2024. That is the value of imports, not total industry sales and certainly not what Britain would save by banning them.

If households bought fewer fireworks, they might spend on a local community event, food or another kind of entertainment instead. They might equally save the money. There is no basis for promising that fewer fireworks would automatically increase jobs, GDP or tax receipts.

But GDP and wellbeing are not the same thing. Treating avoidable injuries and clearing pollution may involve paid work without making society better off. The relevant comparison is between the enjoyment fireworks provide and the harm, resources and opportunities their use consumes.

The practical question is not simply whether to completely ban fireworks and take the joy out of Bonfire Night. It makes more sense to ask which forms of celebration produce the most enjoyment with the least harm. Organised displays, fewer private launches, predictable timings and wildlife-sensitive locations could change that balance. Drone and laser shows might offer alternatives, but they also require electricity and equipment; their sustainability should be assessed, not assumed.

This is especially timely. The government’s fireworks consultation closed in October 2026 after receiving more than 140,000 responses from members of the public, businesses, charities and other stakeholders.

Policymakers now have an opportunity to assess the social costs alongside safety, business impacts and cultural value. A credible assessment would be honest about what the evidence shows, and about the nationwide economic savings that cannot yet be calculated. Because when a fireworks celebration leaves a bill for people who never attended, its market price only tells part of the story.

articles.title: Why so many British pubs are closing down
articles.author: David Bailey, Professor of Business Economics, University of Birmingham
paras: British pubs are disappearing at an alarming rate. Last year around eight closed down every week.
And it’s not simply because people are drinking less. The crisis has been caused by the economics of running a pub.
Our latest research suggests that Britain’s pubs are suffering from rising costs, large debts and the changing priorities of large pub-owning companies.
Of course, the market changes. Younger people are drinking less, online socialising has expanded and supermarkets can sell alcohol at prices that pubs cannot hope to match.

But it is too easy to dismiss so many pub closures as the inevitable consequence of changing tastes. To do so would be to ignore the political choices and financial structures which are making things worse.
We found, for example, that one of the biggest problems has been the rise of large pub companies (known as “pubcos”) since the 1990s.

These firms used a business model in which owning pubs became increasingly detached from brewing beer. Large estates were assembled using substantial borrowing, with the buildings and their future cash flows underpinning the debt.

That model looked attractive when interest rates were low and property values were rising. But it became much more fragile when borrowing costs rose, energy bills soared and customers had less money to spend.
In those circumstances, the pressure to service debt can take priority over a pub’s survival.

The problem is not that every large pub company is badly run, or that debt is inherently wrong. The problem is that a financial model built around property portfolios and debt can create incentives that conflict with the interests of tenants and communities.
It means that a pub can be worth more dead than alive.
The location and land may offer a developer a profitable opportunity to build houses for example. The owner therefore has a financial incentive to sell, even where the business might remain viable.
But the market price of a building does not capture its value to the community.

And where a developer sees a housing opportunity, local residents may simply see the loss of their last meeting place. Once that pub has been converted into flats, the social asset is gone. No amount of nostalgic speeches about British pub culture will bring it back.

Because pubs are not simply businesses selling pints. They are part of the social infrastructure that holds communities together. When the last pub in a village closes, residents lose far more than another place to drink. They lose a place to meet, talk, make friends, support local causes and feel part of a community.

A pub is what social scientists call a “third place”: somewhere beyond home and work where people meet on relatively equal terms. It can host a darts team, a charity fundraiser, a book club meeting or simply the regular who comes in for a chat.

For people living alone, older residents and those at risk of isolation, that ordinary interaction can matter enormously. A pub can also act as a warm space in winter or provide a base for community activities.
These benefits rarely appear on a company’s balance sheet, but they are real.

Here lies the central policy contradiction. Governments routinely celebrate pubs as community hubs, contributors to tourism and anchors of high streets. Yet the tax and regulatory system too often treats them as convenient sources of revenue from alcohol and immovable commercial property.

Business rates have been a particular problem. The latest budget did raise the small business rates threshold offering pubs some relief. But they still face substantial fixed costs regardless of how well they are trading.

Rising wages, national insurance costs, energy bills and alcohol duty add further pressure. Supermarkets, meanwhile, can sell alcohol cheaply and shift much of their business online or into large distribution networks. The result is a playing field that is far from level.

None of this means pubs should receive unlimited public subsidy. Nor should every struggling pub be preserved regardless of whether it has customers or a viable future. But government needs to distinguish between an un-viable business and a valuable community asset being undermined by an unfair cost structure or a speculative property sale.
Britain’s pubs are not just businesses, they are part of the country’s social infrastructure. It is time they were treated that way, before too many more call last orders for the last time.
