articles.title: From industrial powerhouse to uncertain future: lessons from Britain’s chemical industry
articles.author: Janet Godsell, Dean and Professor of Operations and Supply Chain Strategy,  Loughborough Business School, Loughborough University
paras: In 1989 a young Janet Godsell, one of the authors of this article, spent a week on night shifts in the powerhouse at ICI’s Huddersfield works in west Yorkshire. She was starting her career at the biggest chemicals company in the UK, but it would be broken up and sold off a few years later as part of Britain’s drive to focus on only making the most lucrative products. This is the story of what happened to ICI and why its break-up looks less inspired now than it did at the time.
The name “powerhouse” was literal. The building produced the steam and electricity needed across the site, while the works also had its own water and effluent treatment facilities.

The end products were everything from fine chemicals to dyes to synthetic polymers used in making nylon. Engineers, laboratory staff, maintenance teams and apprentices were all based inside the gates. As Janet remembers it, about the only routine job done by an outside company was painting the miles of pipework.

Janet was 18, on a pre-university year before starting an engineering degree that was being sponsored by ICI – or Imperial Chemical Industries as it was originally known. At that age, she wasn’t trying to analyse the company or think about its place in British industrial policy. She simply saw it as enormous, self-contained and slightly otherworldly. On later placements at ICI’s Castner-Kellner works in Runcorn, near Liverpool, the lights, towers and steam seemed to stretch for miles. At night, it looked like a moon base.

The memory that has lasted longest, though, is less dramatic. On her first day at Huddersfield, Janet was with a group of recruits. Some were also bound for university while others were local 16-year-olds starting apprenticeships.

One of the ICI people leading the session brought out a large piece of cardboard with a career path drawn across it – this being the days before PowerPoint. The lines took different routes through practical training, technical college and degrees, then met again when the recruits reached their mid-20s. The message was simple: people might enter the company by different doors, but they could reach the same professional level.

That hand-drawn chart said a great deal about ICI. It not only made chemicals. It connected raw materials, energy, research, factories, skills and communities. It could invest in a teenager and wait years for the return. It could also develop a molecule in a laboratory, work out how to manufacture it safely at scale, and sell it around the world.
Thirty years after ICI was broken up, Britain still has outstanding chemical businesses. The value of its chemical exports kept increasing after inflation until only a few years ago.
Now, however, that has started to change.

The usual account is that the nation lost an old, dirty industry and moved towards a more attractive future based on science and high-value products. It moved away from high-volume, low-margin products like fertilisers, PVC, soda ash and chlorine to focus on areas like pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals and advanced polymers.

Sure enough, modern plants are cleaner, safer and more tightly regulated than the works Janet entered in 1989. But the supporting infrastructure is much thinner. A large company like ICI was vertically integrated, meaning all stages involved in making a product were controlled in-house. Now these activities have been sold to different owners, contracted out, moved overseas or closed.

In other words, Britain did not just shed the less sophisticated parts of chemicals. It also weakened some of the foundations on which the sophisticated parts depended. In an era of protectionism, resource wars and tighter credit, that has become a barrier to growth.
A company, a network and a community

ICI was formed in 1926 from four British chemical businesses that made things like dyes, explosives and bulk chemicals such as acids and halogen gases. Over the following decades the company grew into many other products including fertilisers, plastics, fibres, paints, pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals. Its sites ran through Britain’s chemical heartlands: Cheshire, Lancashire, Yorkshire, Teesside and the Scottish central belt.

The company’s great chemical works were designed as systems rather than collections of stand-alone factories. At Wilton on Teesside, north-east England, large plants made the basic chemicals used by smaller operations on the same site to make products ranging from polythene to perspex (these large and small plants are known respectively as upstream and downstream operations).

The different plants on the site shared everything from steam and power to laboratories, pipelines and treatment facilities. A process that would have been uneconomic on its own might make sense because it supplied several other parts of the site.

This created an early form of what would now be called a circular economy: an output that appeared to be waste on one plant’s financial accounts might be transferred to be used as an input at another site, meaning there was no need to buy it from a third party. Single ownership reduced the contractual and financial barriers to making those loops work.

ICI was unusually serious about developing people, and expected its young engineers to look well beyond Britain. It paid sponsored students to work for their first summer placement at a non-ICI company in a non-English-speaking country. Janet chose to work for Sumitomo Heavy Industries in the outskirts of Tokyo, Japan.

A couple of years later, she returned to Japan for a year as part of her degree to study Japanese. During the final three months, she worked at ICI-Teijin Fluorochemicals, a joint venture between ICI and Japanese chemicals group Teijin that had been established to manufacture a new generation of refrigerants for Japanese carmakers. Few of her colleagues had met a female engineer before.

It’s an example of how ICI’s influence did not stop at the factory fence. It also supported technical colleges, apprenticeships, contractors, sports clubs and social clubs. In some places it provided housing. A large works didn’t just give a town jobs; it helped to forge a sense of identity. When a site closed, much more could vanish than the number of posts on the payroll.

None of this makes ICI a golden age. Janet remembers steaming drains and pollution that would be unacceptable now. Some plants were inefficient or had become commercially unviable. Large companies can also be bureaucratic. But ICI’s big strength was being able to see connections across a whole industrial system. Those connections became easier to overlook when the system was broken into separate businesses.
The attraction of the ‘clever’ end

By the late 20th century, the economics of European bulk chemicals were becoming harder. The manufacturing plants for these products consumed huge amounts of energy and raw material. Newer facilities in the Middle East and Asia often had cheaper feedstocks, greater scale and growing markets close by. To a company like ICI, this was fierce price competition for products whose margins were already thin.

It looked more promising to focus on high-value chemicals. Their value came from patents, specialist science, regulation and close knowledge of customers. In an era where the knowledge economy had become the buzz response to the rise of eastern manufacturing, a small quantity of a successful medicine could be worth more than thousands of tonnes of a basic chemical.

ICI’s 1993 demerger captured the mood. Its pharmaceutical, agrochemical and bioscience businesses became Zeneca, which then merged with Sweden’s Astra in 1999 to form AstraZeneca. A year later, the agribusinesses of AstraZeneca and Swiss pharma giant Novartis were combined to create Syngenta.

Meanwhile a “new” ICI also came out of the demerger that was focused on paints, plastics and bulk chemicals. Four years later, the company borrowed heavily to buy Unilever’s speciality chemicals division. To pay this off, it sold off most of its businesses over the next decade to various buyers. Left mostly with just Dulux paints, the ICI name finally disappeared in 2008 after it was bought for £8 billion by Dutch group AkzoNobel. You can see the whole dismantling of the old conglomerate in the diagram below, along with the status of the different parts of the business today (click to make it bigger).

Hiving off the high-value business was not a foolish strategy. AstraZeneca became one of the world’s leading pharmaceutical companies. Syngenta became a major crop-science business. Britain was right to back science, innovation and higher-value products.

Yet, Janet saw the downsides from the inside. When she finished her degree in 1995, she returned to Macclesfield near Manchester to work for the newly independent Zeneca Pharmaceuticals. The new company was plainly worried about losing the manufacturing excellence it had inherited from ICI. It worked with Warwick Manufacturing Group, an industrial research unit at the University of Warwick, to capture that knowledge and turn it into a more explicit staff training programme.
Britain’s changing chemical export mix, 1997-2023

What began as manufacturing excellence developed into supply chain excellence and helped shape Janet’s own career. Yet this episode gives an insight into what’s at stake when you break up an ecosystem like ICI.

A business can be separated legally and financially in a matter of months. The capabilities that make it work have usually taken years to build. These include experienced people, trusted relationships and routines that are rarely written down in full. The same goes for all the shared equipment and business interdependencies that were taken apart at the same time.
Chemical exports by category (£bn 2023)
The chemicals nobody notices until they are gone

When you hear speeches from politicians about the economy, they rarely talk about ammonia, ethylene, chlorine and industrial solvents. Yet these chemicals that were seen as strategically unimportant to the UK a generation ago are industrial infrastructure in molecular form. Medicines, fertiliser, insulation, packaging, electronics, cars and defence equipment all depend on chains of these basic and intermediate chemicals that most consumers never see.

Billingham on Teesside shows how a chain can narrow while the product at the end still appears to survive. CF Fertilisers, a former ICI business which is today part of US-based CF Industries, permanently closed the site’s ammonia plant in 2023. This was the last ammonia synthesis plant in the UK, following a series of other closures in recent decades. CF now makes nitric acid and ammonium nitrate for its fertilisers from imported ammonia. In other words, fertiliser production remained, but the first stage beneath did not.

CF Fertilisers is now more dependent on overseas ammonia plants, ports, shipping and international prices. Britain has also lost the operating knowledge needed to run a large ammonia synthesis plant. It shows how a capability can disappear even while the factory gate remains open and a familiar product continues to leave the site.

The change is visible in the trade data. As domestic ammonia production has been withdrawn, there’s been a sharp rise in the value of UK anhydrous ammonia imports (meaning ammonia not diluted by water).
UK imports of anhydrous ammonia, 2015-24 (US$ million)

The Wilton works on Teesside shows the same process unfolding across a wider cluster. ICI built the complex in the 1940s so that large upstream plants and smaller downstream operations could feed one another.

In the years since ICI’s demise, individual businesses at Wilton have acquired different owners and some plants have closed. In 2025 the Saudi chemicals firm Sabic confirmed the permanent closure of its Olefins 6 cracker, commissioned by ICI in 1979 to make ethylene gas, among other chemicals. Sabic also owns a nearby polyethylene plant which converted this ethylene into plastic pellets. Now, it’s having to source its feedstock elsewhere.

That can look like a neat move on paper, replacing local ethylene with imported ethylene. In practice, closing a plant also removes a supplier, a contributor to shared costs, and part of the local pool of operators, contractors and engineers. The economics of the remaining plants change, which can make the next closure more likely.

The UK government’s decision in December 2025 to support Ineos’s ethylene operations at Grangemouth in Scotland – this time a former BP business – made the same point from the opposite direction. By then, this was Britain’s last ethylene plant, producing a chemical used across healthcare, food packaging, automotive and aerospace manufacturing.
Ministers rightly described the plant in terms of jobs and critical supply chains, not simply as a private asset. Why does a plant so often become “strategic” only when it is the last one left?

The problem was not Britain’s wish to move up the value chain. It was the belief that the high-value end could be detached from the rest without losing anything important. A single ammonia plant, ethylene cracker or solvent-recovery unit might look poor on its own balance sheet. But that calculation could miss the factories it supplied, the utilities it helped pay for, the skills it sustained and the choices it preserved when imports were disrupted.
What a British chemical works looks like now

A visitor returning after 40 years to one of the old ICI works would recognise the physical outline of a chemical site: tanks, pipe racks, distillation columns, cooling towers, steam and operators in control rooms. The chemistry has not been reinvented because data now travels through digital networks rather than hardwired cables.

Now, however, these are industrial campuses occupied by several businesses. They may still share power, steam, laboratories and so on, but those services are provided through contracts rather than a common corporate hierarchy.

Huddersfield, where Janet’s story began, offers a useful example of how such businesses can make the most of these arrangements. Syngenta, which has been Chinese-controlled since 2017, owns the site and continues to make active ingredients for protecting crops there.

The site’s specialist energy and wastewater infrastructure would be expensive for every new business to reproduce, so Syngenta is opening parts of the estate to companies that can make use of those assets and add something to the local system. Indaver, a Belgian company, is exploring a solvent-recycling facility on the site. The proposal would take industrial waste, recover the solvent acetonitrile, which is used in pharmaceuticals and other complex manufacturing, and return it to Syngenta.
The principle would certainly have been familiar to ICI, albeit now two separate companies must make the relationship work over time.

Northwich in Cheshire, north-west England, provides another glimpse of what modern integration can achieve. Tata Chemicals Europe, the owner of what used to be ICI’s alkalis division, operates a combined heat and power plant that supplies steam and electricity to its own operations and other local businesses. Its carbon-capture-and-use facility takes carbon dioxide from the power plant’s flue gases, purifies it and uses it to make high-grade sodium bicarbonate, which can be used in pharmaceuticals and food production.

The arrangement does not make a gas-fired industrial system impact-free, but it’s an example of an emission from one process becoming a raw material for another – again something very familiar to ICI. The challenge across the British chemicals industry is to recover that instinct while meeting far higher standards on safety, pollution and carbon.

This is vital for today’s focus on circular manufacturing, which is about designing products to be continually reused, repaired, remanufactured or recycled to eliminate waste. Yet the ICI era tells us it must be engineered into sites in ways that make commercial sense.

Indeed, this may be one of the conditions for keeping chemical manufacturing viable in a high-cost economy. European plants cannot always compete with newer overseas facilities on energy or feedstock prices alone. Their advantage may instead come from using less virgin material, recovering expensive solvents, sharing low-carbon utilities and turning residual streams into saleable products.

Those benefits can’t be bought from the other side of the world because they depend on proximity and coordination. A by-product has little value if the potential user is hundreds of miles away, if transport costs exceed its worth, or if the two businesses cannot agree a long-term contract.
The global bargain is fraying
ICI was dismantled because the prevailing supply chain logic was to place each activity where it could be done most cheaply, keep inventories low and use reliable transport to connect the pieces.

This view of business endured for several decades, but the cheapest price at the factory gate was never the whole cost. The real bill also includes transport, tariffs, inventory, finance, regulation, carbon, exposure to energy prices and the risk that a shipment does not arrive when needed. These costs were easy to underplay while energy was reasonably predictable and global logistics worked smoothly.

The 2008 financial crisis began to change the calculation as tighter credit made it more difficult to fund long supply chains and hold inventory. Brexit added friction between UK and European operations.

COVID exposed the risks of concentrated production and lean inventories as lockdowns in China disrupted manufacturing and exports – the UK industry needs China’s yellow phosphorus for agrochemicals, for instance, and pharmaceutical key starting-materials like 6-aminopenicillanic acid (6-APA) for making medicines. Although trade recovered, the concentration of Chinese production leaves manufacturers exposed to future disruption.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine then turned energy and feedstock dependence into an immediate threat to European industry. Russia is a major supplier of palladium, for instance, which is essential for UK pharmaceuticals. Again, the war has exposed the risks of depending on supplies vulnerable to geopolitical tensions.

The 2026 war centred on Iran has provided another sharp reminder. Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz restricted a route used by oil, gas, fertiliser and petrochemical cargoes. For chemical producers, gas is both fuel and a raw material, so a disruption can raise both the cost of running a plant and the cost of what goes into it at the same time.

This shock has arrived when Europe’s position is already weak. Cefic, the European chemical industry body, says Europe’s share of global chemical sales has fallen to 13%, while China accounts for 46%. As recently as 2004, Europe’s share was 28%. The size of the world market has almost quadrupled over that period, but China has taken the lion’s share. Its newer plants, large domestic market and continued investment have put intense pressure on European producers already struggling with high energy costs and weak demand.

In the UK, total UK chemical exports near-doubled between 1997 and the start of this decade after adjusting for inflation. Yet as you can see in the chart below, official production data show a steep fall in chemical manufacturing output after its 2020-21 peak. The Chemical Industries Association estimates that output fell by 60% between 2021 and 2025 and reports at least 25 site closures.
UK chemical manufacturing output 1997-2026

When it comes to chemical capacity within a country, it’s difficult to have a single strategy that will always work best. Spare capacity can look wasteful in normal times and invaluable during a disruption. Keeping every old UK plant open as an insurance policy would have been impossibly expensive over the past couple of decades. Nor is “reshoring” an easy answer. A factory that closed 20 years ago cannot simply be switched back on. Rebuilding needs capital, skills, permits, customers, energy and a network of suppliers.

One argument sometimes used in favour of closing UK chemicals plants is to reduce carbon emissions. But if the same chemical is then imported, the carbon has moved rather than vanished. This is very visible in the UK’s consumption-based greenhouse gas footprint, which measures the carbon emissions from everything a country consumes or buys, regardless of where it’s made. In 2023, the most recent year with reliable data, it was estimated at 699 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, compared with emissions of 384 million tonnes within UK territory.

Chemicals account for only part of that gap, but clearly a national emissions total cannot describe the whole environmental effect of what a country consumes. This doesn’t mean an imported chemical is automatically dirtier. The question is where and how a product is made, what happens if the supply is interrupted, and what else is lost when domestic production ends.

Britain does not need another ICI. The company belonged to a different era. A sensible strategy for the UK today would be selective. It would first identify a limited number of chemicals and capabilities whose loss would expose many other industries.

Examples might include fertilisers, industrial gases, water-treatment chemicals, battery-related materials, or key intermediates used in medicines and advanced manufacturing. This isn’t meant to be a definitive list, but to show the kind of dependency question policymakers need to ask.

The authorities should then support clusters where companies in these fields can share low-carbon power, steam, water, treatment facilities and logistics. They would make more use of solvent recovery, recycling and by-products. And before a major plant closed, those in charge of industrial policy would examine the effect on neighbouring businesses, not just the finances of the owner.

This is harder than choosing between free trade and national self-sufficiency. The work lies in understanding the network well enough to know where a modest intervention could preserve several linked capabilities, and where public money would merely postpone an unavoidable closure.

The people question is just as important. Today’s chemical plants need operators and engineers who can combine deep process knowledge with digital systems, automation and decarbonisation. Once a plant closes and a workforce disperses, they are difficult to recreate.

Britain was right to believe in the clever end of chemicals. The mistake was to imagine that cleverness could thrive forever without somewhere to make things, people who knew how to make them, and an industrial system underneath.

articles.title: Getting a big head start on holiday shopping can benefit retailers and consumers alike
articles.author: James Malm, Professor of Finance and Director of the Global Business Resource Center, College of Charleston
paras: Amazon, Costco, Target, Walmart and other retailers begin their holiday sales as early as October.
But there’s no need to rush to buy wool scarves, fuzzy throw blankets and the other holiday gifts on your list the second you spot some tinsel while shopping.

As a finance professor who studies how people and companies make financial decisions, I can explain why the holiday shopping season starts so early: It can help retailers attract more customers while allowing cash-strapped shoppers to stretch purchases out across multiple paychecks. And, for people with deeper pockets, buying gifts early can help them avoid the stress that goes with last-minute shopping.
Why retailers get such an early start
Estimates for spending on holiday gifts, decor and the like between late 2026 and January 2027 range from about US$1 trillion to $1.7 trillion in the U.S.

Some 29% of Americans plan to shell out their share of those large sums in early to mid-December this holiday season, while 17% will shop on Black Friday, the day after Thanksgiving, according to the Bank of America Holiday Spending survey.

But many people like to shop for holiday gifts early – meaning before Halloween. Some do this out of necessity: They can’t afford to buy all the gifts they want to give unless they spread the cost over multiple paychecks.

For others, it’s more of a preference. In a 2025 survey, about 54% of early shoppers said they want to manage their budgets gradually. In addition, 41% said they buy gifts early to avoid the stress associated with last-minute shopping.

Retailers are adjusting by getting an early start on holiday sales and promoting seasonal items. By offering customers deals months before gift-giving commences, they can encourage even more people to join the early birds.
And by launching promotions in October, they might secure sales that otherwise would go to their competitors later in the season.

A longer selling season offers other advantages to retailers. It may ease pressure on their supply chain and logistics, since they can receive seasonal orders over three months instead of one or two. This minimizes shipping difficulties and lowers warehouse overhead costs.

Building more time into the calendar to move seasonal inventory gives retailers more opportunities to sell those items. However, an earlier shopping season does not necessarily increase consumer spending overall. Some purchases may simply shift from December to October.
Beware of some early-shopping pitfalls
To make sure that buying gifts long before the holidays occur is a wise move, early shoppers should read vendors’ fine print and research their return policies.
Many big retailers are making their return policies more restrictive by shortening the length of time you can return purchases and adding return/restocking fees.

In some cases, the deadline you face for returning an item could fall before the holidays. For example, Best Buy’s extended policy takes effect in 2026 only for purchases made on or after Oct. 30. Target similarly restricts its holiday-season returns window to items bought on or after Nov. 1.

Amazon extended its holiday return policy in 2026. If you buy an item from Nov. 1 to Dec. 31, it can be returned until Jan. 31, 2027, except for Apple products, which can be returned until Jan. 15. Anyone who bought gifts beforehand will likely be subject to a standard 30-day return policy, which will expire long before Christmas.
When buying early makes financial sense
Shopping early is smart when the costs of waiting could outweigh the potential benefits of spending your money earlier than otherwise necessary.

For example, if a popular wool scarf that was priced at $100 in October is out of stock on Amazon by November, the supply is gone, but demand remains high. If you want to buy it for your mom and ensure it arrives in time, you may need to get it from other retailers. Maybe you can find the scarf on a website but is selling for $150. If time has run out, you might have to pay, say, $30 more for expedited shipping, bringing the total to $180. Clearly, you would have been better off buying it early on at a lower price.

But that doesn’t mean you necessarily need to rush to buy a gift weeks or months ahead of when you’ll be placing it under a tree. First make sure that the price is in line with your expectations and what you’re willing to shell out.
And you should do some comparison shopping to make sure other retailers aren’t charging less for the same or similar items.

Remember, waiting to do your holiday shopping until the last minute can lead to unnecessary costs, like rush shipping fees. The key is to have a budget, recognize when the price is right, and know when to stop shopping.

articles.title: Constantly on edge at work? It could be anticipatory stress
articles.author: Sabrina Fitzsimons, Co-Director of DCU CREATE (Centre for Collaborative Research Across Teacher Education), Lecturer in Education, Dublin City University
paras: In Nosferatu (1922), one of cinema’s most haunting images arrives before the vampire himself: his shadow. Something is approaching, but we don’t know exactly what it is, or what will happen when it arrives. The fear lies in the anticipation.
This is called anticipatory stress, and it can affect us in our work lives. An event may be months away, yet psychologically it has already entered the room, casting a shadow on the present.
In my research, I explored the wellbeing at work of university education academics working within high-stakes inspection and accountability systems in the UK and Ireland.

In England, all initial teacher education providers are inspected by Ofsted. In other nations, accreditation inspections may be conducted by professional regulatory bodies, such as the Teaching Council of Ireland. Across these different systems, many academics described feeling anticipatory stress while waiting for an inspection.
Participants in England described living in “constant anticipation”, on “constant red alert” and “on a knife edge” while waiting for the call from Ofsted.

The inspection had not begun, but the expectation of it was already shaping how they worked, where they directed their attention and even how confidently they could make plans outside work. As one participant said, “every family plan is prefaced with, ‘but I could get the call’”.

Anticipation itself is not the problem. It’s a normal psychological function that allows us to prepare for what is coming. The difficulty arises when we know something important is approaching, but our personal control is limited, and we don’t have enough information to decide what useful preparation actually looks like.
Under those conditions, the mind keeps working on the problem. We forecast possible outcomes, we revisit conversations we have had and we can become more attentive to potential signals.

An unexpected request for a meeting or a delayed email response can suddenly acquire particular significance, not necessarily because it means anything, but because uncertainty can make us more vigilant for information that might help predict what comes next.

Psychologists use the term “perseverative cognition” to describe how worry and rumination can keep a potential stressor mentally active when it is not actually present. In simple terms, the stressful event may be absent, but the mind keeps bringing it back into the present.

As one of my interviewees explained: “My mind has already gone into overdrive with worry – even though the inspection might not take place until next year.” Another said: “It’s the ‘not knowing’ that I find so stressful.” Indeed, research into uncertain threat suggests that unpredictability can sustain vigilance, partly because there is no clear point at which we know we can safely stand down.

Many of the events we anticipate at work also carry an element of evaluation. An inspection, promotion process or performance review can place our competence directly under scrutiny, while restructuring may raise a broader question about our future value within an organisation.

Research on social-evaluative threat – the stress we feel when we think we are being judged by others – suggests that these situations can provoke particularly strong stress responses. This was apparent in my own research. “It’s my name up front,” one participant said. “I have led the team so I feel a deep sense of personal responsibility that this goes well for everyone.”
Anticipation is often not only tethered to uncertainty, but to professional identity and the consequences of feeling judged.

My research also showed how the period of anticipation can generate additional work. Many participants noted the gap between official advice and the reality of preparing for a high-stakes event, such as an inspection. Professional bodies might say: “Don’t do anything special for us coming,” but participants felt that, in practice, preparation was unavoidable.

Some described how preparation “almost doubles your workload because you are doing your job and making sure you can demonstrate you are doing the job as well – which is very stressful”. This may be familiar to those in other work contexts. Employees often have to deliver their work while documenting, checking and preparing to account for it. When this preparation takes place in the light of a high-stakes event, it can easily be accompanied by anticipatory stress.

This kind of uncertainty is becoming a familiar feature of organisational life. Restructures are announced before new roles are settled; mergers begin to reshape teams while reporting lines remain unclear.
More recently, new technologies, such as AI, have been introduced while employees are still trying to understand what they will mean for their day-to-day work.

The difficulty isn’t change itself, nor the assumption that the change will necessarily end badly. It is the long period in which people know enough to realise that something important is shifting, but don’t have enough information to make informed decisions or understand their future with any degree of confidence.

Organisations cannot remove all uncertainty from the workplace, and leaders cannot provide answers they do not yet have. They can, however, give uncertainty some boundaries by being clear about what is known, what aspects remain unresolved and when people can expect to know more. Without those boundaries, the period before an important event can fill with worry, rumination and attempts to make sense of incomplete information.

articles.title: Allegheny County is reassessing every property – here’s how your tax bill is calculated now
articles.author: Elizabeth Jane Beckett-Camarata, Professor of Public Administration, Penn State
paras: Allegheny County will undergo a countywide reassessment of every property it taxes for the first time since 2012. A county judge ordered the reassessment in August 2026, requiring the work to begin by July 1, 2027, and finish within five years.

The goal is to bring property values in line with today’s market. That could shift the tax burden among property owners across the county. State anti-windfall rules may require local governments to lower their tax rates after a reassessment to ensure they balance and equalize the tax reassessments. Individual bills may go up or down.

For many homeowners, property taxes are confusing. Terms such as assessment, millage rate and school district tax come up often, but taxpayers may not know what they mean or how each one affects their annual tax bill.
In Pittsburgh, property taxes pay for schools, parks, libraries, public safety and other local services.
I research and teach government finance at Penn State Harrisburg, including a course on state and local taxation. Here’s a plain-language guide to how Pittsburgh’s property taxes work.
What your home is worth – on paper
The first concept is the property assessment. Allegheny County’s Office of Property Assessments gives every property an assessed value. That value is the basis for calculating property taxes.

An assessed value isn’t necessarily what a home would sell for today. Some places, such as Philadelphia, assess property at full market value. Other jurisdictions assess property at a set percentage of market value. In Cook County, Illinois, which includes Chicago, homes are assessed at 10% of their market value. That doesn’t mean Chicago-area homeowners pay less. When assessments are a smaller share of market value, tax rates are set higher to raise the same amount of money. Allegheny County assesses at full value, but it uses what properties were worth in 2012. The court-ordered reassessment is meant to close the gap between those 2012 values and today’s market.

Allegheny County’s 14-year gap would be unusual almost anywhere else. Pennsylvania is the only state that doesn’t require counties to reassess on a regular schedule, while most states do so at least every six years. Within Pennsylvania, though, Allegheny is far from the worst: Butler County hasn’t reassessed since 1969.
Homeowners can look up their assessment on the county’s real estate portal.

Once a property has an assessed value, each local government applies a millage rate to figure out the tax owed. One mill equals $1 of tax for every $1,000 of assessed value. A home assessed at $100,000 has 100 units of $1,000 in value.
Pittsburgh property owners pay property taxes to three government entities: Allegheny County, the City of Pittsburgh and Pittsburgh Public Schools. Each one sets its own millage rate.

For 2026, the city’s general rate is 9.67 mills. The city also charges 0.5 mill for parks and 0.25 mill for libraries. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, and Allegheny County charges 6.43 mills.
Together, those rates add up to 27.307 mills. For a city home assessed at $100,000, that comes to about $2,731 a year before any exemptions or discounts.

The county’s property tax worksheet and the county treasurer’s millage rate page list current rates. These rates are set each year, and all of them will be cut when reassessed values take effect, since the law requires rates to drop as total values rise.
The biggest slice: Schools

School taxes are often the largest share of a homeowner’s property tax bill. In Pennsylvania, property taxes are a major source of revenue for public schools. They help fund salaries for teachers, updates and maintainance for buildings, transportation, and technology and educational programs.

School tax rates vary widely across Allegheny County. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, well below the suburban districts around it. North Allegheny, one of the lowest-taxing suburban districts, charges about 20.4 mills for the 2026-27 school year. Two of the highest are Mt. Lebanon at about 32 mills and Penn Hills at about 32.6 mills. The county treasurer publishes a full list of school district rates.
Help for homeowners and seniors
Some homeowners qualify for programs that lower their tax bills.

The Allegheny County Homestead exemption, known as Act 50, cuts $18,000 from the assessed value of a qualified, owner-occupied, primary residence property’s county taxes. There’s no income limit: Any homeowner who lives in the property as their primary residence qualifies. A home assessed at $100,000 is taxed on just $82,000, which saves about $116 a year. Enrolling in Act 50 also automatically applies Pittsburgh’s $15,000 exemption, which covers the parks and library levies, and a larger Pittsburgh Public Schools exemption that is set each year. Applications for this exemption are due March 1 and need to be filed only once.

The senior citizen tax relief program, known as Act 77, takes another 30% off county taxes for homeowners who are at least 60, have household incomes of $30,000 or less and have owned and lived in their home for at least 10 years. For a qualifying senior with that $100,000 home, the county bill would drop from about $527 to about $369.
If you think your assessment’s too high

Homeowners who believe their assessment is too high can appeal their assessment to the county’s Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. Filing is free; appeals can be submitted online, by email or in person.

Appeals are filed the year before the tax year they affect. The appeal window for 2027 bills closed Sept. 1, 2026. The next window, for 2028 bills, is expected to run from July 1 to Sept. 1, 2027, around the time the reassessment is set to begin.

At an appeal hearing, homeowners can argue their property’s value using either 2012 prices or today’s market. Recent sales of similar homes nearby can help show whether an assessment is out of line. The board can lower the assessment, leave it as is or raise it.
What reassessment means for you

Pittsburgh property taxes come down to two elements: the property’s assessed value and the millage rates set by the county, the city and the school district. Understanding how these elements work together can help homeowners read and comprehend their tax bills and better plan for one of the biggest ongoing costs of owning a home, next to the mortgage payment.

That understanding will matter more as the reassessment gets underway. When new values take effect, some homeowners will see their share of the tax burden rise and others will see it fall. The direction depends on how their property’s value has changed compared with changes of other similar properties since 2012.

articles.title: Are American voters actually gloomy about the economy, or is something else going on?
articles.author: Erin Kay Lockwood, Assistant Professor of Political Science, University of California, Irvine
paras: Polling is looking grim for Republicans ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, 2026, due in large part to deep pessimism among the public about the economy.

At first glance, this might seem surprising. With the exception of inflation, many economic measures remain strong, including gross domestic product growth. But consumer sentiment continues to languish.
This has prompted a debate over whether mere “vibes” are in play, or whether these long-used metrics are no longer capturing something fundamental to Americans’ economic well-being.

This debate matters politically because voters are placing an overwhelming priority on the economy as an issue in the midterms. A Pew Research survey in early October 2026 found that 84% of registered voters said the economy was very important to their vote, and the concern is bipartisan. Among the issues in that Pew survey, for example, “the economy” was the least polarizing, with 82% of Republicans and 88% of Democrats ranking it as very important.

Meanwhile, the overall drop in voters’ economic outlook has largely been driven by growing pessimism among Republicans. While Democrats remain much gloomier about the economy than Republicans, the gap is narrowing.

These trends help explain why Democrats are expected to make significant gains in Congress: This election will likely be seen as an indictment of how well the economy is working for ordinary Americans under President Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress, despite strong macroeconomic measures.

As a scholar of financial markets and global inequality, I believe the relationship between how people see their own finances and their view of the broader economy is also changing on a more fundamental level. And this shift will affect how they judge the next class of lawmakers in power.

When scholars try to understand how people judge the economy – and how they separate their own personal circumstances from the broader economy – one of their key reference points is the University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index. It asks respondents about their personal finances, their short-term and long-term economic outlook, and whether they think it’s a good time to make major purchases.

This gauge has historically tracked key economic measures of consumer spending and inflation: The state of the broader economy usually shapes the way people think about their own financial well-being.
But in recent years, these have diverged. By many measures, the economy is doing well, but people feel they’re falling behind. And this has only become more pronounced ahead of the midterms.
Despite strong consumer spending, robust business investment and low unemployment, consumer sentiment keeps slipping and is now 10% below where it was a year ago, according to the Michigan index.

Some commentators point to ongoing inflation as the reason for gloom. It has remained stubbornly above the Federal Reserve’s annual 2% target rate due to drivers like tariffs, energy price hikes stemming from Middle East turmoil, and massive amounts of investment in the artificial intelligence build-out.

But what’s really happening is that consumer sentiment data and inflation data have become untethered. Inflation has actually dropped sharply from its 21st-century peak of 9.1% in June 2022 after the pandemic to 3.7% in September 2026, but consumer sentiment is lower now than it was even then.

What about wages? Here, too, the data also doesn’t fully explain this disconnect. While inflation makes consumer goods pricier, it also lifts pay. Inflation-adjusted wages actually increased between 2022 and the first half of 2026, all while consumer sentiment remained weak. What has changed in recent months is that inflation-adjusted wages are now falling – which could help explain the darkening outlook among voters.
One possibility is that deeply entrenched inequality explains this divergence.

Compared with other eras of moderate-to-high inflation, the U.S. economy today is much more unequal. Income inequality has increased over the past 20 years, narrowing only during the 2008 and 2020 crises before quickly widening to prior levels.

This trend is important for understanding which consumers are shelling out cash. The Fed has consistently cited strong consumer spending in its economic assessments, but the richest 10% of Americans account for half of that spending today. Meanwhile, spending by the bottom 80% of earners has fallen behind inflation.

In other words, the strong total consumer spending figures reported as official data are being driven by very wealthy Americans and fail to reflect the experience of typical consumers who are the bulk of the electorate.

This trend of increasing inequality has been particularly acute in terms of wealth: The top 0.1% of American households together own five times as much wealth as the bottom 50%. Much of this reflects the uneven gains of the stock market boom and how wealth is taxed.
In short, Americans’ economic malaise might be driven by concerns over income and wealth that conventional measures don’t fully capture.
When it comes to consumer surveys like the University of Michigan index, economists generally assume that the answers reflect the personal experience of respondents.

But I agree with other scholars who argue that sometimes these answers may be based less on people’s own circumstances and more on how they view the economy as a whole. This assessment could reflect, for example, concerns like equity, equality of opportunity and economic justice.
When responses are driven by a concern for collective well-being rather than just personal material self-interest, social scientists refer to such perceptions as “sociotropic.”

This last point isn’t just theoretical. Research suggests voters tend to weight their perceptions of the economy more heavily than their personal financial circumstances when deciding whether to vote for the incumbent party.

Trade is one good example. Americans’ preferences for trade policy are driven less by how a particular measure, like tariffs, would impact them personally and more by how they think it would affect the country as a whole.

If consumer sentiment follows a similar path, that could explain the divergence between generally strong economic trends and weak consumer sentiment. People are thinking not just about their own conditions but those of the U.S. as a whole, and it’s possible that their understanding of “the economy” includes its relationship to inequality.

Understanding the disconnect between the economic data traditionally used to assess the economy’s health and Americans’ perceptions of that economy is important not just to the scholars trying to make sense of it – it could also help set an agenda for the incoming Congress. If economic insecurity punishes the governing party at the polls, the next Congress will be expected to do something about it once sworn in.

Voters generally back the incumbent party when the economy is doing well and the out-party when it’s not. But how they judge the health of the economy is not straightforward, and the past six years suggest that improving headline measures of economic health – without regard to Americans’ lived experience and their concerns about what kind of economy is being built – may not be enough to assuage voters’ concerns.

articles.title: The government has delayed the toughest spending decisions – but here’s what we do know after the budget
articles.author: Steve Schifferes, Honorary Research Fellow, City Political Economy Research Centre, City St George's, University of London
paras: John Healey’s steady-as-she-goes budget was a picture of a government doing its best to offer “what help we can afford”, while weathering the economic storms. But despite its 98 policy measures, decisions on some of the biggest issues appear to have been kicked down the road.

In the meantime, it seems that the real incomes of UK households could fall by 1% next year. This forecast, from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), offered a grim picture. It also predicted UK economic growth of just 1%, as well as higher inflation and interest rates. The OBR, the government’s independent spending watchdog, has also suggested that by 2029-30 households will still be only 1% better off than they were ten years previously. This would be the slowest growth in real disposable household income for generations.

And in further bad news for households, the OBR estimated that the tax collected by the government as a percentage of GDP would reach record levels by 2030-31 – six percentage points higher than pre-pandemic levels. Taxes are already higher than at any time since the second world war.

The budget was enthusiastically backed by Labour members. But it can also be seen as a holding operation by the chancellor, reassuring the markets while leaving the prime minister the space to develop his vision of the causes close to his heart. These of course include social care, devolution and welfare reform. Notably, the only measure which in relative terms was generously funded was the £500 million allocated to end rough sleeping, the cause Burnham cited as his priority on his first day in office.
The limited measures to help with the cost of living reflect Burnham’s concerns about tackling the issue that most worries the public, but they are modest in scale and for the most part temporary.

The Treasury’s modest ambitions are reflected in the limited scale of the additional taxes it has announced to fund cost-of-living measures, especially to help with energy prices. The government has found some taxes it can raise and some efficiency savings it could make.

However, most of the cost-of-living measures – which will cost £6.5 billion this year – are only temporary, while some of the tax increases occur later in the parliament. As a result, the government expects that within five years the situation will be reversed, with Treasury revenues up by £7 billion.

One move that could have a long-term impact is Healey’s changes to the spending rules to protect “preventive spending” from department cuts. These are measures that have an initial cost but eventually save money. An example is the SureStart childcare programme, for example, which has been shown to improve long-term education prospects and reduce crime in deprived communities.
Back to welfare and defence

But the government has postponed its most difficult decisions – on defence, social care, devolution and welfare spending. The latter, the most politically challenging, awaits the publication of two key reports on welfare next month. The Timms and Milburn reviews will report respectively on personal independence payments, and the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet).

Any big decisions are likely to take shape after the publication of the prime minister’s ten-year plan (expected in December), and next year’s spending review, which will flesh out spending plans up to the next general election.

The urgent need to boost defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030 was the issue that led Healey to resign from the previous government. In his first budget as chancellor, despite insisting this target would be met, he was cagey on how it might be financed.

He cited “innovative financing measures”, which might include off-the-books contributions from the private sector through PFI (private finance initiatives) and the use of government investment banks, which may not be subject to the same fiscal rules. Healey also sees defence spending as part of the government’s industrial strategy, and ministers have announced that foreign firms that win defence contracts of more than £50 million will have to deliver benefits of the same amount back into the UK.

Another thing we do know is that defence investment will also be funded by forcing all other departments to cut their own spending by 1%. This is a pattern Healey may repeat to fund other new spending commitments.

In fact, the OBR estimates that, after taking into account the future spending plans of the “protected” departments (health, education and defence), all other departments would need to cut their own spending by 2.6% to allow the government to meet its 2030-31 fiscal target. This would mean less for roads, prisons, the police, housing, and higher education. “Efficiency savings” would be unlikely to close the gap.

The chancellor has taken over at a particularly difficult time for the world economy, and European nations are among the hardest hit. Healey will need luck as well as skill to navigate the shoals of a global slowdown. However, it is already clear that the prime minister’s desire for closer ties with Europe to boost growth is not shared by the chancellor.

Many events – from a resumption of full-scale warfare in the Strait of Hormuz to the possible collapse of the AI bubble – are beyond Healey’s control. He has temporarily reassured the bond markets with his cautious “do no harm” budget. But delivering improved living standards and better public services to a still-jaundiced electorate remains an enduring challenge.

articles.title: Massive sinkholes open up across Turkey as it struggles with drought and climate change
articles.author: Nima Shokri, Adjunct Professor, Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH), United Nations University; Technical University of Hamburg
paras: Turkey’s central Anatolian plateau is one of the country’s most important agricultural regions, producing wheat, maize, sugar beet and other crops. Yet beneath its cultivated fields, the ground is becoming increasingly unstable.
Large sinkholes, some tens of metres wide and deep, have appeared across the Konya basin, swallowing farmland, and threatening nearby roads and settlements.
These collapses can occur suddenly, sometimes in fields that have been cultivated for generations. Around 20 are opening up every year, according to a recent study.
Known locally as obruks, sinkholes are not a new geological phenomenon. They have existed in the Konya basin for thousands of years, but they have become far more frequent over recent decades.

Konya’s sinkholes are consequently both a geological hazard and evidence of a wider water-management problem. The cavities beneath the fields are the product of geological processes extending over thousands of years. Their recent instability, however, is occurring within a groundwater system profoundly altered by human activity and increasingly exposed to drought.

As representatives of countries all over the world prepare to head to Turkey to discuss climate change at the UN’s Cop 31 conference, Ankara continues to grapple with this escalating environmental disaster at home.
The nation’s disaster and emergency management authority (AFAD) has recently documented 684 sinkholes across Konya, Karaman and Aksaray in Turkey’s agricultural heartlands.
The growing number of sinkholes is often attributed to drought and climate change. But intensive groundwater extraction for agriculture can also increase the risk of collapse.

Decades of intensive agricultural irrigation have altered the conditions beneath the basin’s surface. Groundwater, which is the layer of water below the Earth’s surface, is also not being replenished during long, dry periods, which adds to the problem.

Konya is a closed drainage basin. This means water entering the basin does not flow towards the sea. It is stored underground, and accumulates in lakes and wetlands, or returns to the atmosphere through evaporation and plant transpiration.

Rainfall is relatively low here, and much of it falls outside the main growing season. Groundwater has, therefore, become indispensable to agriculture, particularly for irrigated maize, sugar beet and fodder crops.

The difficulty is that demand for water has grown beyond the rate at which the aquifers, a body of porous rock or sediment saturated with groundwater, can recover. A recent regional study estimated an average annual loss of groundwater storage, equivalent to 3.4 centimetres of water. This figure clearly points to a system under sustained pressure.
Part of the problem is that Turkey experienced its most severe drought for decades in 2025, putting more pressure on farmers.

Farmers often respond by extracting more groundwater, causing underground water levels to fall. This reduces the pressure exerted by water within the pores and fractures of rocks and sediments, potentially destabilising existing underground cavities and increasing the risk of collapse.

The consequences extend beyond water scarcity, because groundwater also puts stress on underground geological formations. The Konya basin contains extensive carbonate rocks, including limestone. Over long periods, groundwater circulating through fractures dissolves minerals and enlarges openings. This process, known as karstification, can produce underground channels, caves and cavities. Sinkholes form when the material above such voids becomes unstable.

Lower groundwater levels can also change the movement of water and sediment through existing underground cavities, allowing loose material to shift downwards. Where the roof of a cavity is already weak, these changes may eventually lead to collapse.

But the response is highly dependent on local conditions. The depth and shape of underground cavities, the thickness and strength of the layers of rock and sediment above them, the distribution of fractures and the history of groundwater fluctuations all matter.

This helps explain an important finding from a study on sinkhole formation in the Konya basin between 2000 and 2024. The researchers identified a sharp increase in the annual formation rate, from approximately three sinkholes a year during 2000-10 to 32 during 2016-19. Yet the rate subsequently declined to around 22 a year after 2020, despite continuing groundwater depletion.

If falling groundwater is responsible, why would fewer sinkholes form while water levels continue to decline? One possible explanation is that the most vulnerable cavities in some areas have already collapsed. Sinkhole formation depends on the number of unstable underground structures, not simply on the volume of water extracted.

The basin is also experiencing another type of ground deformation, known as land subsidence, in which the surface gradually sinks as underground sediments compact. This can cause cracks in the ground and damage to roads and buildings, although the sinking is often too gradual to notice without satellite measurements.

Satellite radar measurements revealed widespread land subsidence in the area, of up to 90 millimetres per year. Unlike sudden sinkhole collapse, this can develop as groundwater withdrawal increases stress on the land and compresses sediments in the ground.

The problem is not unique to Turkey. A global analysis estimated that over 6.3 million square kilometres of land are subsiding by more than five millimetres annually. The researchers identified groundwater extraction as the most influential factor worldwide.

In Konya, the pressure on groundwater is closely connected to agricultural production. Farmers cultivate crops for established markets and processing industries, often under policies that have favoured high levels of production, rather than water conservation.
Irrigation provides a way for farmers to maintain yields of crops during dry years, but it also allows production to continue at levels that the basin’s renewable water supply may not sustain.

However, restricting how much groundwater is extracted without providing support for farmers could impose substantial economic pressure on them, as well as on the nation’s food supply. But continued groundwater depletion could progressively undermine the agricultural production that made the region economically important in the first place.

More efficient irrigation could help, but is not enough. If water saved through improved technology is used to expand the area being irrigated, total groundwater consumption may remain unchanged or even increase.

A long-term response would require reliable monitoring of groundwater levels and withdrawals, enforceable extraction limits, agricultural incentives aligned with local water availability and detailed mapping of geological hazards. Satellite measurements can help identify areas under pressure.
The most immediate danger is that another field, road or building may collapse, putting lives at risk.

Preventing the next sinkhole is difficult. The government could address the problem. But it needs to introduce agricultural policies that treat groundwater as a finite resource, rather than a permanent substitute for rainfall.
Nima Shokri is affiliated with Hamburg University of Technology.

articles.title: How different election results affect bank stability – global study
articles.author: George Kladakis, Lecturer in Finance, University of St Andrews
paras: Recent elections in Brazil and Israel have yielded different political outcomes. In Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s narrow and ultimately surprise victory in a presidential runoff vote has kept him in office.

In Israel, meanwhile, an inconclusive election result has left uncertainty over the formation of the next government. These outcomes are likely to have an effect on the stability of the financial systems in both countries.

Historically, financial experts believed elections primarily caused brief, nervous jitters in national stock markets. As prior evidence shows, the impact of political uncertainty is often concentrated around the election period, with short-lived spikes in market volatility.
But our 2026 study of 147 national elections across 22 OECD economies between 2000 and 2023 reveals a much deeper, longer-lasting reality.

To understand this, we must first demystify a common banking term: systemic risk. This is the financial equivalent of a domino effect. It is the danger that a shock to one institution or sector could trigger a widespread collapse across the entire financial system.

We saw this in action on a large scale during the 2008 global financial crisis. At that time, the distress of a few highly interconnected institutions threatened to bring down the entire global financial system. Massive government intervention was required to stop the dominoes from falling.

Our findings show that systemic risk follows a broadly hump-shaped trajectory. It dips before scheduled elections, then rises during and after the vote. The risk remains elevated for up to 12 months, particularly when the incumbent government loses office.

Pre-election spending that supports economic activity, alongside possible government suppression of adverse information about economic and financial conditions, offers an explanation for the temporary calm observed before elections.
How elections affect systemic risk

Our study suggests that political continuity can be a financial asset for national banking systems. But Brazil’s recent experience nevertheless shows that continuity does not automatically reassure investors.

Lula reversed a first-round election deficit of more than 2 million votes to secure his reelection. This was the first time since Brazil’s 1985 return to democracy that a president has managed to overturn a first-round defeat.
So the result surprised markets that had positioned for Lula’s challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, to take office.

On October 26, the day after the runoff vote, Brazil’s benchmark stock index fell 13.9%, while its currency lost 8.1% against the US dollar. There was a modest recovery the following day, with stocks gaining around 1%.

The immediate market reaction does not suggest a banking crisis is underway in Brazil. Whether it develops into broader financial instability depends on how financial institutions and borrowers absorb the shock.

Our study also found that elections that yield no clear winner raise systemic risk, as they leave policy uncertainty over budgets and regulation unresolved. Israel has long struggled to establish durable governing coalitions, and its October 27 election left neither main bloc with a parliamentary majority.

While the US president, Donald Trump, had openly endorsed Israel’s incumbent prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, some investors had been positioning for a change of government. The inconclusive result has unsettled markets that had anticipated a clearer political outcome.

During trading on October 28, the day after the election, Israeli stocks fell around 3%. Israel’s currency, the shekel, also weakened by approximately 2% against the US dollar. And the ten-year government bond yield rose nearly five basis points to 4.13%, signalling higher borrowing costs.

Finally, our data shows that snap elections are associated with larger increases in systemic risk. Here, again, Israel is an instructive example. Israel experienced ten elections between 2000 and 2023, seven of which were snap elections. This included five snap elections during its 2018-22 political crisis.
Strong economic growth and high public trust in government cushion the financial blow of elections, as they naturally insulate the banking system.

Macroprudential policies, the regulatory guardrails designed to protect the entire banking system, also play a crucial role. By strengthening financial safeguards such as capital buffers for banks, regulators can help the system absorb political shocks.

Unfortunately, evidence suggests that political incentives to stimulate lending before an election can encourage the loosening of these safeguards. This leaves national financial systems more exposed to subsequent shocks.
In Turkey and India, for example, governments have historically used state-owned banks to expand consumer and mortgage credit aggressively before tightly contested elections.

This creates a short-term boost in economic activity and voter goodwill, but often leaves the financial system vulnerable to a hangover of non-performing loans and instability once the votes are counted.

As well as being political events, elections are macroeconomic shockwaves. While the stock market might experience a brief spike in volatility on election night, the true test lies in the systemic risk that lingers in the banking sector for months afterwards.

In Brazil, Lula eventually secured backing from voters for a fourth presidential term. Strengthening financial stability there after this surprise result will require rebuilding market confidence with a credible fiscal plan that explains how campaign promises will be funded and puts public debt on a sustainable path.

In Israel, prospects for a viable government remain uncertain. And even if one emerges, it may offer markets only limited reassurance while the war in the Middle East continues to pose risks to financial stability in Israel and worldwide.

articles.title: Faculty and students show how reporting is done when a university partners with local news
articles.author: Teri Finneman, Professor of Journalism, University of Kansas
paras: Catherine Bilskie, the advertising and office manager for the newspaper in Solon, Iowa, had seen many local news outlets close. So she was sure her job at the Solon Economist was about to go one Friday morning in February 2024.

But to her surprise, a new owner, Jason Brummond, appeared. He not only promised to keep her and her co-worker employed at the weekly paper but assured them raises if they agreed to an unusual new venture. And he wasn’t a wealthy benefactor or a representative from a private equity firm – he came from the University of Iowa.

It’s just one example of academic institutions stepping up to address the “news desert” crisis: Thousands of communities across the U.S. have lost local newspapers over the past two decades. And journalism faculty, staff and students are increasingly working together to either rescue legacy newspapers or start new publications for communities lacking local news outlets.

These partnerships have ranged from the Spanish-language news site Noticiero Móvil at the University of Nevada, Reno, to “Good Morning Indian Country” at the University of Kansas, to The Scope at Northeastern in Boston.

We’re journalism professors who have studied and experienced the opportunities and challenges of running community news through higher education. Our new book, “News Desert U,” asks whether this approach is one solution to saving local news. We believe the need is urgent given the stakes and the scope of the crisis.
These experiments come against a grim backdrop.

Over 3,000 newspapers have closed in the U.S. in the past 20 years, including about 170 in 2025, according to Northwestern’s 2026 State of Local News report. Causes include an antiquated business model, declining advertising revenue and hedge-fund buyouts that have gutted papers. Northwestern’s 2025 report estimated that total print newspaper circulation has declined 70% in the past 20 years.
But university partnerships can show promise, we found, with the help of the next generation of journalists.

Iowa’s Solon Economist is one example. The University of Iowa doesn’t actually own the paper, or its sister paper, the Mount Vernon-Lisbon Sun. Still, the relationship is key to making the new venture work.

Its owner, Brummond, is also the publisher of the University of Iowa’s student newspaper, the Daily Iowan, which is owned and operated by the nonprofit Student Publications. While the student newspaper office is inside the journalism school’s building, it operates independently.

In August 2023, Student Publications began talks about buying the Sun and the Economist after the weeklies’ then owner reached out about selling the publications. With both newspapers 20-30 minutes from campus, discussions included how the faculty and students could help the papers.

The Journalism School’s director, Melissa Tully, was immediately in favor – provided that the newspapers’ existing professional staff stay and not be replaced with students. In addition to the editors, this included keeping the advertising and circulation staff.

“They know these communities. So that was really important just from a moral and ethical imperative, but also from a news perspective,” she said. “They’re trusted in their communities. They know what’s going on.”

Student Publications bought both newspapers for US$10,000 in 2024. Since then, circulation has remained stable at both, Brummond said, even as many other publications across the country have suffered declines.
Meanwhile, students in classes such as community news, high school sports, social media marketing and photography contribute for academic credit while other students do paid internships.
Solon Economist Editor Chris Umscheid said he welcomes a revolving door of student interns because it means he’s “actually going to have staff for once.”
“People thought we were going to be the university’s paper, and we’re not,” he said. “I don’t anticipate anything changing there. We’re still going to focus on everything Solon that we can.”

The success has led to Student Publications getting requests to buy other newspapers, Tully said, and it’s working on a list of criteria to consider future partnerships. Brummond cautions these arrangements aren’t easy to pull off, as they require a careful review of finances, workflow and logistical complications that come with a merger.
Liz King, who served as Solon Public Library director, said many locals were afraid the newspaper would close, which would have been a hard blow for the town of about 3,000.
Some readers only get their news through the newspaper, she said. “They’re not comfortable with online sources.”
Dink NeSmith had a similar close scare in Georgia with the The Oglethorpe Echo.

Owner Ralph Maxwell had decided in September 2021 that he had no choice but to shutter the paper due to his own health issues, revenue declines and lack of interest from prospective buyers. He gave NeSmith, an old friend and retired newspaper owner, an early heads-up.
“I don’t know that I want to live in a town that doesn’t have its newspaper,” was NeSmith’s response. He told Maxwell: “You can’t close the Echo.”
NeSmith immediately reached out to the University of Georgia’s journalism school to suggest a partnership.

In the meantime, NeSmith worked to set up a separate nonprofit, Oglethorpe Echo Legacy, for the paper’s new ownership structure. Keeping the newspaper’s finances independent of the university was an important step to ensure the paper would not be subject to any possible “whims” of future administrations, as Charles Davis, the journalism school’s dean, put it. That status was also a signal to Oglethorpe County that the paper’s goal was to serve the community, not make money, he added.
The new nonprofit bought the paper from Maxwell in October 2021 for $10 – a check that Maxwell never cashed and has since been framed.

Davis asked Andy Johnston, an adjunct professor with decades of journalism experience, to serve as the newspaper’s full-time editor. Since November 2021, Johnston has led a team of journalism faculty and students, with the help of several adult staff and volunteers from the county.

The paper covers a wide terrain. Oglethorpe County has over 16,000 people stretching over 442 square miles, and Lexington, where the Echo has its office, is 18 miles (29 kilometers) from the campus in Athens. The reporting staff is provided by journalism professor Amanda Bright’s capstone class – 20 students each semester. Supplementary funding comes from the journalism school, various grants and Echo subscription and advertising funds.

She pairs two students to each beat, with one in charge of a story and the other in charge of editing and producing, with a rotation each week. Students need to turn in eight stories a semester – with corresponding editing and producing assignments that include video, an email newsletter and social media – to get class credit.

When the journalism school took over, the weekly had only a printed newspaper, with no website, social media presence or other digital products, she said. So in their first print edition, the editors outlined their plan for the newspaper to readers and then introduced the student reporters, which they still do every semester.

The partnership has paid off. Print subscriptions to The Echo have doubled and overall digital audience has quadrupled thanks to the launch of new digital products, Bright said. Advertising revenue, meanwhile, has tripled, she said. However, it took some time for local businesses to get used to advertising again, NeSmith said.

But many challenges remain. Johnston has to handle student turnover every semester while students covering events such as government meetings face a steep learning curve and need support. The additional time it takes to edit student copy means content doesn’t appear as quickly. Many faculty members have to work long hours to keep the paper afloat.
But the broader impact is clear: More than two dozen students have gone into local news as a career following their time at the Echo, Bright said.

Should other universities want to follow this model, they need at least two key people in leadership, whether that’s two faculty members or one from faculty and a professional editor, Bright said. “That’s a bottom-line necessity for sanity,” she added.
One common theme from our research is that a service-oriented approach to news that addresses the community’s needs takes priority over profit at these partnerships.

The built-in advantages for these initiatives is that the faculty and staff who tend to manage them get their paychecks and health insurance from their university work. They don’t need to draw a living wage from the news outlet’s finances.

These partnerships are also ideal for students seeking real-world experience while earning class credit or internship wages. And journalism schools are already stocked with multimedia equipment that students can use for their reporting.

Still, they can look deceptively simple on the surface, Brummond said. Tully, at the University of Iowa, recommends other interested universities should go slowly. Building a successful project takes patient experimentation and a willingness to regroup when needed, in her view.
“Doing this slowly is OK,” she said. “In the end, it’s going to be better. So far, that’s been a good recipe for us.”
Teri Finneman and Pamela Walck are co-authors of the book "News Desert U."
